slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Ditch That Runs Your Life
slide1.body: A 193km canal in Egypt moves 15% of all global trade. One ship, one sandbank, one bad day — and the world economy starts sweating.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Suez Canal, Egypt
slide2.body: 193km long. 24m deep. No locks — it's flat the entire way. It cuts through Egypt connecting the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, saving ships a 9,000km detour around Africa.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: ~$9.6 Billion of Cargo. Every Single Day.
slide3.body: ~15% of world trade passes here. The laptop you're reading this on. ~8% of global LNG. 1 in 8 containers shipped on Earth. European car parts from Asia. All through a gap 313 metres wide.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: One Ship Got Stuck. It Cost $60 Billion.
slide4.body: March 2021. Ever Given wedged itself sideways. 369 ships queued. ~$400M per hour frozen. Meanwhile Houthi attacks since 2023 have already diverted ~40% of normal Suez traffic the long way around Africa.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Europe: electronics delayed 2–3 weeks, prices creep. Egypt: loses ~$700M/month in canal fees. India: household gas prices spike within days. Everyone: shipping insurance doubles overnight.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Strait That Could Break The World
slide1.body: 39km wide at its narrowest point. 21% of the world's oil squeezes through here every single day. Iran has one hand on the tap.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Hormuz
slide2.body: Between Iran and Oman. Ships travel in a 3km-wide lane each way — narrower than many city rivers. ~21 million barrels of oil pass through daily. There is no alternative route.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: 21% of Global Oil. Zero Alternatives.
slide3.body: Japan imports ~85% of its oil through here. India gets ~60% of its crude this way. South Korea, China, Taiwan — all critically dependent. The next closest route adds 15 days and $2M per tanker.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Iran Has Threatened To Close It 4 Times This Decade
slide4.body: The US 5th Fleet patrols it full time. Iran's Revolutionary Guard has speedboats and sea mines on standby. Every Israel–Iran escalation puts this strait back in the headlines. One incident = global fuel crisis in days.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Japan: emergency oil reserves last 90 days max, then the lights start going out. India: petrol prices spike within 72 hours. Germany: chemical plants start rationing in 3 weeks. Everyone: inflation.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Busiest Sea Lane On Earth
slide1.body: More ships pass through the Strait of Malacca than any other waterway. It connects the Indian Ocean to the Pacific. Half the world's trade in goods moves through it.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Malacca
slide2.body: Between Malaysia and Indonesia, 800km long, narrows to just 2.7km at the Singapore end. ~90,000 ships per year. That is one ship every 6 minutes, 24 hours a day.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Half Of Global Trade In Goods. One Narrow Gap.
slide3.body: ~80% of China's oil imports pass through here. Same for Japan and South Korea. The iPhones, the Nikes, the cheap electronics — all of it sails through a lane narrower than some urban motorways.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Pirates, Congestion and One Very Nervous China
slide4.body: It was the world's most pirated waterway until aggressive naval patrols in the 2000s. Now the threat is congestion and China–US tension. Beijing calls its dependence on this strait the 'Malacca Dilemma' — and it keeps them up at night.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: China: oil reserves last ~80 days, then factory output collapses. Japan: ~80% of energy imports vanish overnight. Southeast Asian ports: economic implosion within weeks. Global electronics: delayed 2–4 months minimum.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Strait Nobody Could Spell That Broke Global Shipping
slide1.body: Bab el-Mandeb. Gate of Grief in Arabic. The Houthis turned it into exactly that for every major shipping company on Earth in 2023.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Bab el-Mandeb, Yemen/Djibouti
slide2.body: 30km wide between Yemen and Djibouti, at the bottom of the Red Sea. ~10% of global trade passes through here on the way to or from the Suez Canal. Yemen sits on the eastern shore.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The On-Ramp To The Suez Canal.
slide3.body: Every ship going from Asia to Europe via Suez has to pass through here first. ~6 million barrels of oil daily. Close this and the Suez Canal itself becomes largely irrelevant — there's nothing to let through.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Houthi Missiles Have Already Rerouted 40% Of Suez Traffic
slide4.body: Since October 2023 the Houthis have attacked 100+ ships. Maersk, MSC, CMA CGM, BP all rerouted via Cape of Good Hope. The detour adds 10–14 days and ~$1M in fuel per voyage. This is not hypothetical. It is happening now.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Europe: consumer goods and car parts delayed, prices rising. Egypt: Suez Canal revenues down ~40%, a fiscal crisis in slow motion. Global shipping: freight rates up 200–300% since late 2023. Everyone: higher prices on almost everything.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Canal That Shortened The World By 13,000km
slide1.body: Before the Panama Canal, ships sailed around the entire continent of South America. Now they take an 80km shortcut through a country that barely existed when it was built.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Panama Canal, Panama
slide2.body: 80km long, connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans through Panama. Uses a series of locks that physically lift ships 26 metres above sea level and lower them back down. ~14,000 ships per year.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: ~5% of World Trade. The US–Asia Connection.
slide3.body: ~40% of all US container traffic passes through here. LNG from the US Gulf Coast to Asia. Grain from the US Midwest to the world. Without it, the alternative adds 13,000km around South America.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Climate Change Is Already Closing It. Partially.
slide4.body: 2023 drought reduced the canal's reservoir by 40%. Panama cut the number of daily ship transits by 36%. Ships queued for weeks. Some rerouted. The canal runs on rainwater — and there is less of it every year.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US East Coast: consumer goods from Asia delayed weeks. Asian LNG buyers: rerouting costs passed on to energy bills. US grain exporters: $100M+ in delays in 2023 drought alone. Global shipping: unpredictable and getting worse annually.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Europe's Back Door Is Only 14km Wide
slide1.body: The gap between Europe and Africa is narrower than many cities. Every ship entering the Mediterranean squeezes through here.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Gibraltar
slide2.body: 14km at its narrowest, between Spain and Morocco. The Atlantic meets the Mediterranean. ~100,000 ships per year — about one every 5 minutes.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Every Ship To Mediterranean Europe Goes Through Here.
slide3.body: Oil, grain, cars, electronics. All of it. Southern Europe's entire seaborne trade funnels through 14km of water. No alternative route exists.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Spain And Morocco Have Fought Over This Before
slide4.body: The 2002 Perejil Island crisis saw Spanish commandos recapture a tiny Moroccan-occupied rock 200m from the shipping lane. NATO patrols it. Migration crises regularly spike tensions.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Italy, Greece, Turkey: cut off from Atlantic trade. Spain: ~60% of imports arrive by sea through here. North Africa: export routes to Europe vanish. Global shipping: massive Mediterranean reroute via Suez adds weeks.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: A City Built On Top Of The World's Most Strategic Waterway
slide1.body: Istanbul sits on the only route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Russia's entire naval access south runs through a Turkish city.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Bosphorus Strait, Istanbul
slide2.body: 700 metres wide at its narrowest. A city of 15 million people on both banks. ~50,000 ships per year. Bridges carry motorway traffic directly over the shipping lane.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Russia's Only Warm-Water Naval Route. Controlled By NATO.
slide3.body: ~3% of global oil. Ukraine's entire grain export corridor. Russia's Black Sea Fleet must pass through Turkish waters to reach the Mediterranean. Turkey controls the tap under the 1936 Montreux Convention.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Turkey Closed It To Russian Warships In 2022
slide4.body: When Russia invaded Ukraine, Turkey invoked the Montreux Convention and blocked Russian warships from transiting. Russia's Black Sea Fleet was trapped. This is not hypothetical — it already happened.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Ukraine: grain exports choked, food prices spike globally. Russia: naval power projection cut in half. Romania and Bulgaria: trade routes to the Mediterranean severed. Global wheat: immediate shortage signals.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Backup Route When Everything Else Breaks
slide1.body: When the Suez Canal gets blocked, the Houthis attack Red Sea shipping, or any other crisis hits — every ship reroutes 9,000km around the bottom of Africa.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Cape of Good Hope, South Africa
slide2.body: The southwestern tip of Africa. Where the Atlantic and Indian Oceans meet. In 2023-24, Houthi attacks forced ~40% of Suez traffic to reroute here, adding 10-14 days per voyage.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: It Becomes Critical Exactly When Everything Else Fails.
slide3.body: Not usually a chokepoint — it's open ocean. But when the Suez or Bab el-Mandeb closes, this becomes the only route for Asia-Europe trade. In 2024, daily cargo volume here jumped ~200%.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Already Handling 40% More Traffic Than Normal
slide4.body: Since Houthi attacks began in late 2023, the Cape route has been overwhelmed. Port congestion in Cape Town. Insurance for routing here doubled. Shipping companies paying ~$1M extra per voyage in fuel alone.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Europe: 10-14 extra days on every Asia import. South Africa: sudden port congestion, infrastructure strain. Global shipping: ~$1M extra fuel cost per round trip. Retailers: just-in-time supply chains break.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Strait Between Bali And The Island Next Door Controls Asia-Australia Trade
slide1.body: Between Bali and Lombok. Deep enough for aircraft carriers and supertankers. China's main alternative when Malacca gets complicated.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Lombok Strait, Indonesia
slide2.body: Between Bali and Lombok islands. 40km wide but unusually deep — unlike Malacca, supertankers and aircraft carriers can transit without depth restrictions. Used as an alternative to Malacca.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: China's Backup Plan If Malacca Gets Blocked.
slide3.body: ~100 ships per day. Critical for Australian iron ore exports to China. US Navy uses it regularly to move carrier groups between Pacific and Indian Ocean. If Malacca closes, Lombok carries the overflow.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Indonesia Controls It. And Indonesia Is Watching China Very Carefully.
slide4.body: Indonesia has disputed maritime boundaries with China in the South China Sea. Any escalation puts Indonesian control of Lombok — and the transit rights it grants — directly in play.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Australia: iron ore exports to China delayed or rerouted. China: oil imports from Middle East forced through longer routes. US Navy: carrier group movements constrained. Global LNG: major disruption to Australia-Japan flows.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Strait With A Volcano In The Middle
slide1.body: Sunda Strait sits between Sumatra and Java. Krakatau — one of the most violent volcanoes in history — sits in the middle of the shipping lane.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Sunda Strait, Indonesia
slide2.body: Between Sumatra and Java, connecting the Indian Ocean to the Java Sea. 24km at its narrowest. Anak Krakatau volcano active in the shipping lane. Third busiest strait in Southeast Asia.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Southeast Asia's Third Busiest Shipping Lane.
slide3.body: ~60 ships per day. Alternative route when Malacca is congested. Critical for LNG from Australia to Northeast Asia. Indonesian domestic shipping — the world's largest archipelago state — depends on it.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: An Active Volcano In The Shipping Lane. Literally.
slide4.body: Anak Krakatau erupted and collapsed in 2018, triggering a tsunami that killed 400+ people. Ships transiting during activity must reroute. Seismic risk is constant. This is a geological threat, not just a political one.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Indonesia: domestic inter-island trade disrupted. Australia: LNG exports rerouted. Northeast Asia: energy imports delayed. Singapore: overflow congestion when Malacca traffic diverts here.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Russia's Pacific Fleet Has To Ask Japan's Permission — Sort Of
slide1.body: The Tsugaru Strait is the only deep-water passage between Japan's two largest islands. Russia and China both need it to move ships between the Pacific and Sea of Japan.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Tsugaru Strait, Japan
slide2.body: Between Honshu and Hokkaido islands. 19km wide. Under international law, it's an international strait — Japan can't close it — but it patrols every transit closely.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Only Deep Route Between Two Japanese Seas.
slide3.body: Russia's Pacific Fleet uses it regularly. China's naval exercises in the Pacific often transit here. Japan monitors every single passage. In a US-China conflict scenario, Japan's position here becomes decisive.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: China Sent Warships Through Here In 2021. Japan Lodged A Formal Protest.
slide4.body: A Chinese carrier group transited in October 2021. Japan scrambled aircraft and issued a formal diplomatic protest. The legal right to transit exists — but Japan makes clear it's watching.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Russia: Pacific Fleet access to warm waters constrained. China: naval exercises in Pacific complicated. Japan: any closure triggers US-Japan alliance response. Regional trade: disruption to Japan-Russia LNG flows.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The World's Widest Chokepoint That Nobody Talks About
slide1.body: 450km wide and yet — it's a chokepoint. The Mozambique Channel is the main route for oil tankers from the Gulf to South Africa and South America.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Mozambique Channel, East Africa
slide2.body: Between Mozambique and Madagascar. 450km at its widest, 400km long. One of the main routing options for tankers heading from the Persian Gulf to South Africa, Brazil and the South Atlantic.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: South Africa's Oil Lifeline. Also Massive LNG Reserves Below It.
slide3.body: ~30 tankers per day. South Africa imports ~65% of its oil through here. Massive offshore LNG fields discovered in northern Mozambique. And it's increasingly a piracy corridor.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: ISIS-Affiliated Insurgency Controls Territory On The Northern Shore
slide4.body: Since 2017, an Islamist insurgency in Cabo Delgado province (northern Mozambique) has attacked LNG infrastructure. Total SA suspended a $20B LNG project. Armed groups active near the shipping lane.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: South Africa: fuel shortages within weeks. Mozambique: LNG revenue lost, $20B investment frozen. Brazil: oil imports from Gulf rerouted at significant cost. East Africa: regional trade disrupted.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: A Bridge Connects Two Countries. Below It: Russia's Access To The Atlantic.
slide1.body: The Øresund bridge connects Denmark and Sweden. Underneath it, the only route out of the Baltic Sea for Russian, Finnish, Swedish and Estonian ships.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Øresund Strait, Denmark/Sweden
slide2.body: 4km wide between Copenhagen and Malmö. A motorway and railway bridge span the exact shipping lane. ~100,000 ships per year. Russia's Baltic Fleet must transit to reach the North Sea.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Every Baltic State's Trade Exits Through NATO Territory.
slide3.body: Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Germany — all Baltic trade exits through Danish-controlled straits. Russia's Kaliningrad enclave logistics run through here. Denmark controls access.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Russia's Baltic Fleet Is Effectively Locked In By NATO Members
slide4.body: Since Finland and Sweden joined NATO in 2023-24, Russia's Baltic Fleet is surrounded. Denmark controls Øresund. Any wartime scenario sees Russia's Baltic naval forces unable to exit without transiting multiple NATO states.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Russia: Baltic Fleet trapped if NATO closes straits. Baltic states: trade bottleneck in any crisis. Germany: ~25% of trade goes through Baltic ports. Finland, Sweden: newly critical NATO strategic assets.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Most Dangerous 180km Of Water On Earth
slide1.body: The Taiwan Strait separates China from Taiwan. It carries ~half of global container traffic. Both sides have missiles pointed at each other across it.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Taiwan Strait, East Asia
slide2.body: 180km wide between mainland China and Taiwan. ~50% of global container ships transit annually. The US Navy patrols it. China considers it sovereign territory. Taiwan disagrees.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Half Of Global Container Traffic. Plus 90% Of Advanced Chips.
slide3.body: Taiwan makes ~90% of the world's most advanced semiconductors. A blockade doesn't just stop ships — it stops every laptop, phone, car, and weapons system that needs cutting-edge chips. For years.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: China Fired Missiles Over Taiwan In 2022. Ships Rerouted.
slide4.body: During Nancy Pelosi's visit, China fired ballistic missiles over Taiwan. Major shipping companies quietly rerouted. Insurance rates spiked. This wasn't a drill — ships physically changed course.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Everyone with a phone, laptop or car: chip shortage within months, lasting years. Japan and South Korea: immediate energy and trade crisis. US: semiconductor supply for defense systems compromised. Global GDP: economists estimate -10% scenario.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: North Korea's Missiles And South Korea's Exports Share The Same Waters
slide1.body: The Korea Strait connects the East China Sea to the Sea of Japan. South Korea's entire export economy transits here. North Korea fires missiles over it.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Korea Strait, East Asia
slide2.body: Between South Korea and Japan. Split by Tsushima Island. ~400 ships per day. Busan — the world's 6th largest container port — sits on its northern shore.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Busan: World's 6th Largest Container Port Sits Right On It.
slide3.body: South Korea exports ~$600B/year — semiconductors, cars, ships, electronics. The vast majority exits through this strait. Japan's western coast trade depends on it. North Korean provocations directly threaten it.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: North Korea Fired A Missile That Flew Over Japan Through This Airspace In 2022
slide4.body: In October 2022, North Korea fired an ICBM that overflew Japan. Ships in the Korea Strait received emergency alerts. Insurance rates spiked. The strait is directly in the shadow of North Korean missile tests.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: South Korea: export economy paralysed. Japan: western coast ports shutdown. Samsung, Hyundai, LG: production and shipping halted. Global chip supply: major disruption alongside Taiwan scenario.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: China's Navy Has To Pass Through Here To Reach The Pacific
slide1.body: The Luzon Strait is the main deep-water passage between the South China Sea and the Pacific Ocean. US and Chinese submarines play cat and mouse through it constantly.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Luzon Strait, Philippines/Taiwan
slide2.body: Between Taiwan and the Philippines. 250km wide. The primary deep-water exit from the South China Sea into the Pacific. US carrier groups and Chinese submarines both transit regularly.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Door Between China's Near Seas And The Open Pacific.
slide3.body: Chinese naval doctrine calls this the 'First Island Chain' — the barrier it wants to break through. Every Chinese submarine heading to the Pacific must transit here. US forces are watching every single one.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Multiple US-China Military Confrontations Have Happened In These Waters
slide4.body: Chinese warships have repeatedly crossed within dangerous distances of US vessels here. In 2023, a Chinese destroyer cut across a US destroyer at 137 metres. The strait is actively contested.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Philippines: caught between two superpowers in their own waters. Taiwan: encirclement complete if China controls this passage. US Pacific strategy: severely complicated. Global shipping: South China Sea routes closed.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Mediterranean's Waist. Split It Here And You Cut Europe In Half.
slide1.body: The Strait of Sicily divides the Mediterranean into eastern and western basins. Oil from Libya, migrants from North Africa, and NATO submarines all transit through 145km of water.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Sicily, Italy/Tunisia
slide2.body: 145km wide between Sicily and Tunisia. Splits the Mediterranean into two halves. ~2,000 ships per week. Libya's oil exports transit here. Europe's migration crisis passes through it.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Libya's Oil, Italy's Energy, Europe's Migration. All Here.
slide3.body: ~30% of Mediterranean oil trade passes through. Italy depends heavily on Libyan gas. NATO's southern flank runs straight through it. The migration route from North Africa to Italy crosses it daily.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Libya's Civil War Has Put Armed Militias On Both Shores
slide4.body: Libya has had two competing governments since 2014. Militias control the coastline. Oil pipelines are weaponised. Russia has positioned Wagner Group forces near Libyan ports. Italy is 145km away.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Italy: gas imports disrupted, energy crisis. Malta: completely surrounded by this strait. North Africa: trade routes to Europe severed. NATO southern flank: strategic vulnerability exposed.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Russia Built A Bridge Over Ukraine's Sea Access. Then Blew It Up.
slide1.body: The Kerch Strait connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov. Russia built a bridge over it in 2018. Ukraine blew it up in 2022. Control of this 4km gap determines whether Ukraine has a functioning sea port.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Kerch Strait, Crimea/Russia
slide2.body: 4km wide between Crimea and mainland Russia. Connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov. Russia's 2018 Kerch Bridge — the longest in Europe — spans it. Ukraine attacked it twice in 2022-2023.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Ukraine's Sea of Azov Ports Are Completely Controlled From Here.
slide3.body: Mariupol and Berdyansk — Ukraine's main Azov Sea ports — can only be reached through the Kerch Strait. Russia blocked Ukrainian ships here in 2018. Since 2022, the entire Sea of Azov is a war zone.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Ukraine Hit The Kerch Bridge With A Truck Bomb In 2022 And A Missile In 2023
slide4.body: October 2022: truck bomb damaged the bridge. July 2023: Ukrainian missiles hit it again. Russia's main supply route to Crimea severed twice. Each attack directly affects shipping through the strait.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Ukraine: Azov ports completely inaccessible. Russia: Crimea resupply severely disrupted. Global grain: Ukrainian Azov port exports (significant wheat volume) blocked. Black Sea shipping: insurance impossible to get.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Only Exit From The Gulf Of Mexico
slide1.body: Every barrel of oil from the Gulf of Mexico, every LNG tanker from US Gulf ports, every container from Houston — they all have to squeeze through the Yucatán Channel to reach the world.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Yucatán Channel, Mexico/Cuba
slide2.body: 210km wide between Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula and Cuba. The only deep-water exit from the Gulf of Mexico. US Gulf Coast energy exports, military vessels, and Caribbean trade all transit here.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The US Gulf Coast's Only Door To The World.
slide3.body: Houston is the largest port in the US by tonnage. US Gulf LNG exports (~$50B/year) exit here. Gulf of Mexico oil platforms export through here. Any disruption strands the entire US energy export economy.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Cuba Sits On One Side. Instability There Directly Affects US Energy Exports.
slide4.body: Cuba controls the eastern shore. A political crisis in Cuba — or any hostile act by a regional power — puts US energy export infrastructure in range. The US military watches this channel extremely closely.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US: energy export revenue choked. Gulf Coast states: economic crisis. Europe: LNG imports from US reduced, energy prices spike. Caribbean: import-dependent islands cut off. Global LNG market: immediate price shock.

slide6.headline: 81 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the Americas edition has more chokepoints than you'd think.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Miami And Havana Are 160km Apart. Between Them: A Major Shipping Lane.
slide1.body: The Florida Strait runs between the US and Cuba. It carries the Gulf Stream, major shipping lanes, and has been the site of military confrontation since 1962.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Florida Strait, USA/Cuba
slide2.body: 160km between Florida and Cuba at the narrowest. Carries the Gulf Stream — a major ocean current affecting European climate. ~15,000 ships per year including major container routes from the Caribbean.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Every Ship From The Caribbean To The US East Coast Uses This.
slide3.body: Major container routes from Panama Canal to US East Coast transit here. Caribbean energy imports flow through. US Navy's Atlantic fleet exits through this corridor. Cuba's position makes it permanently strategic.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: The Cuban Missile Crisis Was Partly About Control Of This Strait
slide4.body: In 1962, Soviet missiles in Cuba could threaten every ship in the Florida Strait. The US naval blockade was enforced here. Today, Cuban instability and potential Chinese naval access to Havana keeps US planners focused on this gap.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US East Coast: Caribbean imports disrupted. Caribbean islands: cut off from North America. Panama Canal traffic: major rerouting required. Florida economy: direct impact given port dependence.

slide6.headline: 80 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Cold War geography that's still very much live.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: US Submarines Take This Route. So Does Cocaine.
slide1.body: The Windward Passage between Cuba and Haiti is a major US Navy transit corridor and the primary drug trafficking route from South America to the United States.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Windward Passage, Cuba/Haiti
slide2.body: 80km wide between eastern Cuba and northwestern Haiti. Primary US Navy route between Atlantic and Caribbean. ~5,000 ships per year. Haiti — currently in gang-controlled chaos — sits on one shore.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: US Naval Submarines Transit Here Regularly. So Does ~40% Of Caribbean Drug Traffic.
slide3.body: US Strategic Command uses this passage for submarine movements. DEA estimates ~40% of cocaine heading to the US passes through this corridor. Haiti's complete state collapse makes the eastern shore ungoverned.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Haiti Has No Functioning Government And Gang Control Of Its Coast
slide4.body: As of 2024, gangs control ~80% of Port-au-Prince and significant stretches of coastline. Ungoverned coastline adjacent to a major US naval corridor is a security nightmare.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US: drug interdiction efforts severely compromised. Caribbean: instability spreads from Haiti. Regional trade: disruption to Caribbean shipping. US Navy: security risks on a key transit route.

slide6.headline: 79 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — where geopolitics, narcotics and naval strategy share the same 80km of water.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Most Treacherous 800km Of Ocean On Earth Is Also A Shipping Lane
slide1.body: The Drake Passage between South America and Antarctica is the stormiest ocean on the planet. Before the Panama Canal, every ship from Atlantic to Pacific had to survive it.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Drake Passage, Southern Ocean
slide2.body: 800km wide between Cape Horn and Antarctica. The only open ocean route between Atlantic and Pacific. When Panama Canal or other routes fail, ships face the Drake — 40-foot waves, hurricane-force winds, icebergs.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: It's The Last Resort Route When Everything Else Fails.
slide3.body: Panama Canal drought, Suez crisis, any major disruption — ships can always go around Cape Horn. Just very slowly and dangerously. Antarctic research supply, fishing fleets, and cruise ships use it regularly.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Climate Change Is Making The Drake More Unpredictable
slide4.body: Warming oceans are destabilising Antarctic ice and creating more extreme weather in the Drake. Icebergs are increasingly appearing in shipping lanes. The route that ships use 'when nothing else works' is getting harder.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Global shipping: last-resort route becomes more dangerous. Antarctic research: supply missions threatened. Chilean/Argentine fishing: major industry faces increased risk. Falkland Islands: resupply routes affected.

slide6.label: FOLLOW FOR MORE
slide6.headline: 78 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — including the one where the main threat is a 40-foot wave, not a missile.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Magellan Found This Route. Chile Controls It. Argentina Is Not Happy.
slide1.body: The Magellan Strait cuts through the bottom of South America. Chile owns both shores. Argentina has contested this. The world's southernmost shipping lane.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Magellan, Chile
slide2.body: 560km long through Chilean Patagonia. Connects Atlantic and Pacific south of the continent. Chile uniquely controls both shores. Calmer than Drake Passage but still brutal. ~8,000 ships per year.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Chile Controls The Only Calm Alternative To The Drake.
slide3.body: For ships that can't survive Drake Passage conditions, Magellan is the only alternative. LNG carriers from Atlantic to Pacific use it. Chilean salmon and copper exports depend on it. Argentina-Chile border disputes extend into the strait.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Chile And Argentina Nearly Went To War Over The Beagle Channel Next Door In 1978
slide4.body: Argentina and Chile came within hours of war in 1978 over nearby islands. Pope John Paul II mediated. The border dispute in these waters has never been fully resolved. Chile's sovereign control of Magellan remains contested in spirit.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: South America: Atlantic-Pacific trade disrupted. Chilean exports: copper and fish trapped. LNG carriers: forced to use more dangerous Drake route. Argentine economy: loses alternative to Atlantic-Pacific transit.

slide6.headline: 77 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Patagonia edition: beautiful, freezing, and surprisingly contentious.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Gallipoli Was Fought Over This Waterway. It's Still Worth Fighting Over.
slide1.body: The Dardanelles connects the Aegean to the Sea of Marmara — and onward to the Bosphorus and Black Sea. In WWI, the entire Gallipoli campaign was an attempt to seize control of it.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Dardanelles Strait, Turkey
slide2.body: 61km long, 1.2km at its narrowest. A WWI battlefield. Now 48,000 ships per year transit, including Russia's oil exports and Ukraine's grain. Turkey controls both shores.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Russia's Oil Exports. Ukraine's Grain. All Through 1.2km Of Turkish Water.
slide3.body: ~3 million barrels of oil per day transit. ~25% of Russian oil exports pass through. Ukraine's Black Sea grain exports (when not blocked by war) must pass here. Turkey literally controls a tap on Russian energy revenue.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Turkey Has Used This As Leverage Against Russia Multiple Times
slide4.body: Montreux Convention (1936) gives Turkey full control. In 2022, Turkey blocked Russian warships after the Ukraine invasion. Russia, dependent on this route for oil revenue, cannot retaliate without risking the income stream.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Russia: oil exports choked, immediate revenue loss. Ukraine: grain exports blocked in wartime. Bulgaria and Romania: Black Sea trade bottlenecked. Turkey: extraordinary leverage but extraordinary responsibility.

slide6.label: FOLLOW FOR MORE
slide6.headline: 76 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Ottoman geography still runs the world.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Strait Of Messina Is 3km Wide. A Proposed Bridge Would Span The Whole Thing.
slide1.body: Between Sicily and mainland Italy. The narrowest point is 3km. Italy has been debating building a bridge across it for 60 years. In the meantime, ~80,000 ships per year squeeze through.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Messina, Italy
slide2.body: 3.1km at its narrowest. Between Sicily and the toe of the Italian boot. Strong currents and eddies make it technically demanding. The 'Scylla and Charybdis' from Homer's Odyssey.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Sicily's Only Connection To The Italian Mainland.
slide3.body: 5 million people on Sicily depend on ferry connections through the strait. ~80,000 ships per year including Suez Canal traffic. Italian rail connects to Sicily via ferry. Any closure isolates Europe's largest island.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: The 1908 Messina Earthquake Killed 200,000 People Here
slide4.body: One of the most seismically active areas in Europe. The 1908 earthquake destroyed Messina and killed 75,000-200,000 people. A major earthquake today would close this strait for months and isolate Sicily.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Sicily: 5 million people isolated from mainland. Italian mainland: major traffic disruption. Mediterranean shipping: congestion around Sicily rerouting. Tourism: Sicily's economy collapses without ferry connections.

slide6.label: FOLLOW FOR MORE
slide6.headline: 75 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Homer was writing about real geopolitics.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Internet For Half The World Runs Through These Cables Off Oman's Coast
slide1.body: Multiple major undersea cables connecting Europe, India, Southeast Asia and East Africa land on Oman's coast. Cut them and half the world's internet traffic goes dark.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Undersea Cable Hub, Oman Coast
slide2.body: Multiple cables — AAE-1, SMW5, EIG, FALCON — land along Oman's coast. Together they carry a significant portion of traffic between Europe, Middle East, India and Southeast Asia.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Europe-India Internet Traffic, Banking, Military Comms. All Through These Cables.
slide3.body: Financial transactions, military communications, cloud services, consumer internet. India processes ~$800B in annual digital trade. Europe-Asia business communications. All of it runs through cables on the seafloor here.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Houthi Forces Cut Three Cables In The Red Sea In February 2024
slide4.body: In February 2024, three major undersea cables (AAE-1, Seacom, EIG) were cut in the Red Sea — likely by Houthi activity. Internet speeds across East Africa and parts of Asia dropped ~25%. This is no longer hypothetical.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: India: internet latency spikes, financial transactions delayed. East Africa: internet crippled. Europe: some degradation of Asia connectivity. Global finance: routing disruption for transactions clearing through affected nodes.

slide6.label: FOLLOW FOR MORE
slide6.headline: 74 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the internet has chokepoints too, and nobody is guarding them.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Russia's Pacific Energy Exports Depend On A Strait That Freezes Every Winter
slide1.body: The Strait of Tartary separates Sakhalin Island from the Russian mainland. Russia's massive Sakhalin LNG projects export through these waters. In winter, it ices over.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Tartary, Russian Far East
slide2.body: Between Sakhalin Island and the Russian mainland. Partially freezes in winter. Russia's Sakhalin-1 and Sakhalin-2 LNG projects — producing ~10% of Japan's LNG — export through these waters.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: ~10% Of Japan's LNG Comes From Here. In Winter, Ice Blocks Delivery.
slide3.body: Japan gets roughly 10% of its LNG from Sakhalin projects. When the strait ices over, icebreakers are required. Russia's control of this route is leverage over Japan's energy security — and Russia knows it.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Russia Used Sakhalin Energy As Leverage After Japan Sanctioned It Over Ukraine
slide4.body: After Japan joined Western sanctions in 2022, Russia threatened to nationalise Sakhalin-2 (which it then did). Japanese companies Mitsui and Mitsubishi faced losing ~10% of Japan's LNG supply overnight.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Japan: energy crisis if Sakhalin LNG cut off. South Korea: partial exposure to same supply. Russian Far East: economic isolation deepens. Global LNG market: significant supply shock.

slide6.label: FOLLOW FOR MORE
slide6.headline: 73 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — including several that ice over in winter, which adds a whole new dimension.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Climate Change Is Opening A New Shipping Route. Russia Controls It.
slide1.body: The Arctic is melting. A new shipping lane between Europe and Asia is opening up along Russia's northern coast. It's 40% shorter than Suez. Russia charges transit fees and can close it at will.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Northern Sea Route, Arctic Ocean
slide2.body: Along Russia's Arctic coastline from Murmansk to the Bering Strait. 40% shorter than the Suez route for Europe-Asia trade. Currently only navigable ~3-4 months per year. Climate change is extending that window.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: A 40% Shorter Europe-Asia Route. Opened By Climate Change. Owned By Russia.
slide3.body: Europe to Japan via Suez: 21,000km. Via the Arctic: 12,800km. For shipping companies, that's millions saved per voyage. Traffic has grown from 4 ships in 2010 to 35+ in recent years. Russia controls every transit.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Russia Requires All Ships To Hire Russian Icebreaker Escorts And Pay Transit Fees
slide4.body: Russia's Nuclear icebreaker fleet is the world's largest — built specifically to control this route. Foreign warships are banned without Russian permission. Russia can close the route to any nation it chooses.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Europe: loses access to a shorter Asian trade route. Arctic environment: accelerating ice loss from increased traffic. China: major investor in Arctic route development — freezes if Russia-West tensions escalate. NATO: new northern flank vulnerability.

slide6.label: FOLLOW FOR MORE
slide6.headline: 72 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some chokepoints are opening as others close. The Arctic ones are the most geopolitically chaotic of all.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Canada Says It's Their Internal Waters. Everyone Else Disagrees.
slide1.body: The Northwest Passage through Canada's Arctic archipelago is opening as ice melts. Canada says it's sovereign territory. The US, EU and China say it's an international strait. Nobody agrees.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Northwest Passage, Canadian Arctic
slide2.body: Through Canada's Arctic islands, connecting Atlantic and Pacific north of the continent. Mostly ice-free for 1-2 months per year now. Shortens Europe-Asia Pacific routes. Canada claims full sovereignty.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: A New Arctic Route With Zero Rules And Multiple Nations Claiming Control.
slide3.body: If fully navigable, cuts Europe to Pacific trade routes significantly. Massive mineral and energy resources along the route. US and Canada have disagreed about sovereignty since 1969. Climate change is making it urgent.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: US And Canada Have Disagreed About This Since The USS Manhattan Sailed Through Without Asking
slide4.body: In 1969, the US deliberately sent a supertanker through without Canadian permission to establish freedom of navigation precedent. Canada was furious. The legal dispute has never been resolved — and traffic is increasing.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Canada: sovereignty challenged by world powers. Arctic communities: environmental damage from shipping. Russia: competitive pressure on Northern Sea Route. US: strategic conflict with its closest ally.

slide6.headline: 71 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some of the most consequential chokepoints haven't opened yet. But they're coming.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Battle Of Leyte Gulf — The Largest Naval Battle In History — Was Fought Over This Strait
slide1.body: In 1944, Japan sent its entire remaining fleet through the San Bernardino Strait in a desperate attempt to destroy the Allied invasion of the Philippines. It failed. The strait is still strategically critical.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: San Bernardino Strait, Philippines
slide2.body: Between Luzon and Samar islands. Deep-water channel into the Philippine Sea from the west. US Navy uses it regularly. China's naval expansion increasingly brings warships to these waters.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Critical Access Point Between South China Sea And Pacific.
slide3.body: Alternative deep-water route alongside Luzon Strait. US carrier groups use it. Chinese naval exercises regularly probe it. In any South China Sea conflict, controlling these Philippine straits is essential to naval dominance.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: China Has Sent Warships Through Philippine Waters Without Notice Multiple Times
slide4.body: Chinese naval vessels have transited Philippine waters claiming innocent passage rights. The Philippines has filed formal protests. Under the US-Philippines mutual defence treaty, these transits carry alliance implications.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Philippines: sovereign waters contested. US: alliance credibility at stake. Regional trade: disruption to Philippine archipelago shipping. Regional stability: any incident here risks broader South China Sea escalation.

slide6.label: FOLLOW FOR MORE
slide6.headline: 70 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — WWII was partly fought over the same straits that matter today.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Japan Sent Its Last Battleships Through Here. They Were All Sunk.
slide1.body: Surigao Strait was the site of the last battleship-vs-battleship naval engagement in history. 1944. Japan lost everything. The strait still controls access between the Pacific and Philippine Sea.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Surigao Strait, Philippines
slide2.body: Between Leyte and Mindanao. 25km wide. Southern entrance to the Philippine Sea from the Mindanao Sea. Alternative transit for vessels avoiding the more contested northern straits.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Southern Philippine Maritime Access Point.
slide3.body: Controls access from Mindanao Sea to Pacific. Philippine domestic shipping depends on it. Any conflict in the South China Sea creates pressure on all Philippine straits as alternative transit routes.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Mindanao — On Its Southern Shore — Has Had Active Insurgencies For 50 Years
slide4.body: The Bangsamoro region of Mindanao has seen decades of insurgency. Abu Sayyaf pirate groups have operated in these waters. Instability on one shore creates maritime security risks in the strait.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Philippine domestic trade: disrupted. Mindanao economy: isolated. Regional fishing: affected. International shipping using southern Philippines routes: increased security costs.

slide6.label: FOLLOW FOR MORE
slide6.headline: 69 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the Philippines has more strategic straits than any country its size.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: US Submarines Use This Route. The Indonesian Navy Has No Idea When.
slide1.body: The Ombai Strait is deep enough for submerged submarine transit. US nuclear submarines use it regularly to move between the Pacific and Indian Ocean undetected. Indonesia has not consented.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Ombai Strait, Indonesia/East Timor
slide2.body: Between Indonesia's Lesser Sunda Islands and East Timor. Deep enough for submerged submarine transit — critical. Used by US and Australian submarines moving between ocean basins without surfacing.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: One Of Three Deep-Water Straits Submarines Can Transit Submerged.
slide3.body: Malacca is too shallow for submarines. Ombai, Lombok and Sunda are the main deep-water routes. US Pacific Command depends on these for moving submarines between oceans without China detecting them.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Indonesia Is The World's Largest Muslim Country And Does Not Want To Pick Sides
slide4.body: Indonesia's foreign policy is strictly non-aligned. US submarines using its waters without permission is technically illegal. Indonesia knows this happens. It's a diplomatic fiction everyone maintains.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US Pacific strategy: severely disrupted if Indonesia closes access. Australia: defence posture dependent on these transit routes. Regional security: China would love to know exactly when submarines transit here.

slide6.headline: 68 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some chokepoints are submarine highways nobody talks about.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Iran Has A Port, A Missile Base And A Mine Depot Next To The World's Most Critical Waterway
slide1.body: Bandar Abbas — Iran's main naval base — sits directly on the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guard speedboats launch from here. It's not just a threat. It's a loaded gun pointed at 21% of global oil.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Bandar Abbas / Qeshm Island, Iran
slide2.body: Iran's main Persian Gulf port and naval base. The Revolutionary Guard's naval headquarters. Qeshm Island sits in the middle of the strait. Iran controls the northern shore of the world's most critical chokepoint.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Iran Doesn't Need To Close Hormuz To Disrupt It. It Just Needs To Threaten To.
slide3.body: Every time Iran-US tensions spike, oil prices jump. Insurance rates for Gulf tankers double. Ships reroute. Iran has never closed Hormuz — but the credible threat alone moves global energy markets.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Iran Seized A British Tanker Here In 2019 And A US-Linked One In 2023
slide4.body: HMS Stena Impero seized July 2019. MSC Aries boarded April 2023. Iranian speedboats operate with impunity in these waters. Each incident sends insurance rates up and ships into diversion.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Japan and South Korea: immediate energy emergency. India: petrol prices spike in days. Global shipping: insurance costs double on every Gulf voyage. Shipping companies: forced rerouting costs millions per vessel.

slide6.headline: 67 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Iran has turned chokepoint threats into a fine art form.

name: Perim Island / Bab el-Mandeb Northern Channel

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: A Tiny Island In The Middle Of The Strait Controls Which Ships Can Pass
slide1.body: Perim Island sits in the centre of Bab el-Mandeb, splitting it into two channels. Ships in the western channel pass 3km from Houthi-controlled Yemen. The eastern is narrower. There's no good option.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Perim Island, Yemen/Djibouti
slide2.body: A 13km² Yemeni island splitting Bab el-Mandeb into two passages. The 3km western channel is the main lane. Since 2023, Houthi missiles and drones have targeted ships in both lanes.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Ships In The Western Channel Are 3km From Houthi Missile Launchers.
slide3.body: ~$9B of cargo passes through daily. Houthis have fired anti-ship missiles and drones since October 2023. ~90+ ships attacked. Every major carrier has rerouted. The western channel — the main lane — is a shooting gallery.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Houthis Hit A US-Owned Ship With A Ballistic Missile In January 2024
slide4.body: The MV Zografia was hit by a Houthi ballistic missile in January 2024. US and UK airstrikes on Houthi positions followed. The attacks have not stopped. Multiple ships have sunk or been abandoned.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Global shipping: freight rates up 200%+. Egypt: Suez revenues down 40%. European consumers: higher prices on Asian imports. Energy markets: LNG rerouting costs. Insurance industry: war risk premiums at record levels.

slide6.headline: 66 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some chokepoints are currently active war zones. Bab el-Mandeb is one of them.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Busiest Shipping Lane In The World Has A 33km Crossing At Its Narrowest
slide1.body: The English Channel carries ~500 ships per day. The Dover Strait — 33km wide — is the world's most congested shipping lane. Every ship from Northern Europe to the Atlantic squeezes through.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: English Channel / Dover Strait
slide2.body: 33km at the Dover-Calais crossing. ~500 ships per day plus ferries and Channel Tunnel traffic. The busiest maritime chokepoint by vessel count anywhere on Earth. UK on one side, France on the other.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: 500 Ships Per Day. Northern Europe's Trade Gateway.
slide3.body: Every container ship from Rotterdam, Hamburg, Antwerp heading to the Atlantic passes through. Britain's imports mostly come through here. Post-Brexit friction at Dover has already caused lorry queues visible from space.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Post-Brexit Checks Have Caused Kilometre-Long Lorry Queues At Dover
slide4.body: Since Brexit, new customs checks have repeatedly caused massive tailbacks at Dover-Calais. Perishable goods ruined. Just-in-time manufacturing disrupted. Political tensions between UK and France play out in a 33km gap.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: UK: import disruptions immediate. Northern European exporters: delays and costs. Just-in-time manufacturers: supply chain collapses. French agriculture: export lorries stuck for days. Both countries lose.

slide6.headline: 65 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some chokepoints are being deliberately complicated by their own governments.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Norway's Entire Oil Wealth Exits Through Here
slide1.body: The Skagerrak connects the North Sea to the Baltic. Every barrel of Norwegian oil, every Norwegian gas tanker, every Scandinavian container ship exits through this gap. Norway is Europe's largest energy supplier.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Skagerrak, Norway/Denmark/Sweden
slide2.body: 160km wide between Norway, Denmark and Sweden. Connects North Sea to Baltic Sea. Norway's oil platforms output flows through here. ~200 ships per day including major LNG tankers.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Norway Replaced Russia As Europe's Biggest Gas Supplier After 2022.
slide3.body: After Europe sanctioned Russian gas, Norway became the continent's largest gas supplier. All of that gas transits through pipelines and tankers passing the Skagerrak. Europe's energy security now runs through Norway — and this strait.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Sabotage Of Nord Stream In 2022 Proved Energy Infrastructure Is Targetable
slide4.body: The 2022 Nord Stream pipeline explosion — still officially unsolved — demonstrated that European energy infrastructure is vulnerable. Norwegian pipelines and tanker routes through Skagerrak are now actively protected by NATO.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Europe: immediate energy crisis if Norwegian exports disrupted. Germany: most dependent on Norwegian gas since Russia cutoff. Nordic countries: regional energy market collapsed. UK: North Sea oil transit disrupted.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: A Failed State On One Side Of A Major Shipping Lane
slide1.body: The passage between Haiti and the Dominican Republic is a major shipping corridor. Haiti — where gangs now control most of the country — sits directly on the western shore. The eastern shore is stable. The contrast is stark.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Haiti/DR Maritime Corridor, Caribbean
slide2.body: The waters between Haiti and the Dominican Republic. Major cruise ship and cargo routes. Haiti's complete state collapse since 2021 has created ungoverned coastline adjacent to busy shipping lanes.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Ungoverned Coastline Creates Piracy And Trafficking Corridors.
slide3.body: Haiti's gang-controlled coasts have seen an increase in maritime crime. Arms trafficking and drug smuggling through these waters. US Coast Guard interception of Haiti-bound arms has increased dramatically since 2021.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Haitian Gangs Now Control 80% Of Port-au-Prince And Much Of The Coastline
slide4.body: Gang confederation G9 and allies control major ports, fuel depots, and coastal areas. Haiti has no functioning police force or coastguard. The shore of a major shipping lane is effectively ungoverned.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Haiti: humanitarian catastrophe, no seaborne aid getting through. Caribbean: instability spreading. Regional shipping: security costs increasing. Dominican Republic: forced to militarise the border with Haiti.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Egypt Closed This Strait In 1967. Israel Started A War.
slide1.body: The Strait of Tiran gives Israel its only Red Sea access. When Egypt blockaded it in May 1967, Israel launched the Six-Day War six days later. The strait has been a casus belli twice in modern history.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Tiran, Red Sea
slide2.body: Between Sinai and the Saudi coast. 13km wide. Israel's only access to the Red Sea and Indian Ocean via the port of Eilat. Saudi Arabia and Egypt both control shores. Multinational peacekeeping force monitors it.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Israel's Only Non-Mediterranean Sea Access. One Blockade = One War.
slide3.body: Eilat is Israel's main port for Asian trade. If Tiran closes, Israel is cut off from the Indian Ocean. This happened in 1956 and 1967. Both times, Israel went to war. The strip of water has never been neutral.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Saudi Arabia Transferred Two Islands In The Strait To Saudi Control In 2017
slide4.body: Egypt transferred Tiran and Sanafir islands to Saudi Arabia in 2017. Israel had to be consulted — proving how sensitive this is. Any change in Saudi stance toward Israel directly affects who controls the strait.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Israel: immediate trade and energy crisis. Jordan: Aqaba port loses Red Sea access. Saudi Arabia: leverage but diplomatic exposure. Middle East: immediate escalation risk from any closure.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Comoros Islands Sit In The Middle Of A Major Shipping Lane And Have Had 20 Coups
slide1.body: The Comoros archipelago occupies a strategic position in the northern Mozambique Channel. It has had more successful coups than any country in the world. Political instability meets critical shipping.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Northern Mozambique Channel, East Africa
slide2.body: Between mainland Africa and Madagascar. ~400km wide but narrows near the Comoros. Major routing option for tankers from Persian Gulf to South Africa and South America. Comoros sits in the middle.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: South Africa's Oil Lifeline. Also An LNG Discovery Zone.
slide3.body: South Africa imports ~65% of its oil through this channel. Huge LNG discoveries off northern Mozambique. Chinese and Indian navies increasingly patrol here. East African trade corridor runs through it.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Comoros Has Had 20 Coups Since Independence. One Involved French Mercenaries.
slide4.body: The Comoros has had 20 coups or coup attempts since 1975 — more than anywhere else. France has intervened militarily. The most famous involved mercenary Bob Denard. Political instability adjacent to a shipping lane is always a risk.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: South Africa: energy supply disrupted. Mozambique LNG: extraction and export threatened. East Africa: regional trade routes destabilised. China and India: competing naval interests in the same waters.

slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the world's coup capital sits in the middle of a shipping lane.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The US Military Calls Guam 'The Tip Of The Spear'. China Has Missiles Aimed At It.
slide1.body: Guam is the US's western-most Pacific territory. It hosts massive military bases that project US power across Asia. China has specifically designed missiles to hit it. In a Taiwan crisis, Guam is target #1.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Guam, Western Pacific
slide2.body: 3,800km from Japan, 2,500km from the Philippines. US Pacific Command's main hub. Andersen Air Force Base and Naval Base Guam host strategic bombers, submarines, and carriers.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Every US Military Response In The Western Pacific Flows Through Guam.
slide3.body: B-52s deploy from Andersen. Attack submarines from Naval Base Guam. Any Taiwan, Korea, or South China Sea conflict requires Guam to function. The US is spending $11.7B upgrading its defences.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: China's DF-26 Missile Is Called The 'Guam Killer' — And It's Deployed
slide4.body: China's DF-26 intermediate-range ballistic missile has a range specifically designed to hit Guam — 4,000km. It's been deployed in significant numbers. In 2020, China's military openly called it the 'Guam killer'.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US Pacific power projection: crippled. Japan and South Korea: exposed without US forward base. Taiwan: defence scenario fundamentally changed. Regional US allies: confidence in extended deterrence shaken.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The World's Most Pirated Waterway — Even After It Got Better
slide1.body: Malacca was so plagued by pirates in the early 2000s that the IMO declared it too dangerous. Then regional navies cracked down. Now it's safer — but piracy never fully went away.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Northern Malacca Strait, Malaysia/Indonesia
slide2.body: The northern approach near Aceh province — historically the most dangerous stretch. 40km wide here, narrowing to 2.7km at Singapore. ~80,000 ships per year transiting a waterway with active piracy history.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Even A Small Piracy Incident Spikes Insurance Rates For 80,000 Ships.
slide3.body: One successful piracy incident in Malacca triggers 'war risk' insurance reviews for the entire strait. That's ~80,000 ships paying higher premiums. The economic impact of instability here is disproportionate.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Modern Pirates Use GPS, AIS Hacking And Social Media To Target Tankers
slide4.body: 21st-century pirates in Malacca are sophisticated. They monitor AIS signals, coordinate via mobile phone, and specifically target anchorage areas. 2023 saw a return of incidents in Indonesian waters of the strait.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Shipping companies: insurance premiums spike immediately. Port of Singapore: congestion as ships slow or reroute. Regional economy: security costs passed on to consumers. China: most exposed as largest user of the strait.

slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — pirates were the original disruptors of global trade.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Albania Mined This Strait In 1946. Two British Warships Sank. International Law Changed Forever.
slide1.body: The Corfu Channel incident is one of the most important cases in international maritime law. Albania mined the strait. British ships hit the mines. The ICJ ruling established the right of innocent passage in straits.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Corfu Channel, Greece/Albania
slide2.body: Between Corfu island and the Albanian mainland. 4km at its narrowest. The 1946 ICJ case about this channel established foundational international maritime law still used today.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Legal Principle That Allows Ships Through Every Strait Came From Here.
slide3.body: The 1949 ICJ judgement in the Corfu Channel case established that international straits cannot be closed to innocent passage — even through territorial waters. UNCLOS is built on this principle. Every ship in every strait benefits from this 4km channel.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Greece And Albania Have Disputed Territorial Waters Here For Decades
slide4.body: Greece-Albania maritime boundary disputes in the Ionian Sea include these waters. An unresolved 1985 Albania-Greece dispute over the area technically means the two countries are technically still in a state of war.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Greece-Albania relations: persistent diplomatic friction. Adriatic trade: any closure affects Italian and Balkan coastal shipping. EU: unresolved border dispute in member state's waters. NATO: two members with unresolved maritime dispute.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Greece And Turkey Have Almost Gone To War Over These Waters Six Times Since 1974
slide1.body: The Aegean is full of Greek islands sitting right next to Turkey's coast. Greece claims the airspace and waters. Turkey disputes it. Both are NATO members who nearly went to war with each other in 1996.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Eastern Aegean Sea, Greece/Turkey
slide2.body: Hundreds of Greek islands within kilometres of the Turkish mainland. Disputed airspace limits, contested islets, grey zones. ~250,000 ships per year. Two NATO members who regularly scramble jets at each other.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Eastern Mediterranean Oil And Gas Discoveries Have Made The Dispute Financially Critical.
slide3.body: Massive natural gas fields have been discovered beneath the Eastern Mediterranean. Who controls the Aegean islands determines who controls the exclusive economic zones — and the gas beneath them. Billions of euros at stake.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Greek And Turkish Jets Had A Dogfight Over The Aegean In 2023
slide4.body: In September 2023, a Greek F-16 and Turkish F-16 had a mock combat engagement over the Aegean. Both pilots were NATO allies. The EU condemned Turkey. Turkey blamed Greece. It happens regularly.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: NATO: alliance credibility damaged by member states fighting each other. Eastern Mediterranean gas: development stalled by unresolved disputes. Turkish exports: Aegean transit creates diplomatic friction. Greek islands: tourism and economy at risk.

slide6.headline: 57 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — NATO has internal chokepoint disputes too.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: One Of The World's Largest LNG Discoveries Sits Beneath One Of The World's Most Unstable Regions
slide1.body: Northern Mozambique holds some of the largest LNG reserves discovered this century. Getting them out requires a stable corridor through a region dealing with insurgency, cyclones, and colonial-era poverty.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Southern Mozambique Channel
slide2.body: The southern portion of the channel between Mozambique and Madagascar. Major route for South African oil imports. Mozambique's LNG fields in Cabo Delgado will eventually export through these waters.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Mozambique's LNG Could Supply Europe After Russia Cutoff — If They Can Get It Out.
slide3.body: Europe desperately needs alternatives to Russian gas. Mozambique's offshore fields could supply ~40 billion cubic metres annually. Total SA has $20B invested. The insurgency in Cabo Delgado has stalled everything.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: ISIS-Linked Insurgents Destroyed The Town Of Mocímboa Da Praia In 2020
slide4.body: Ansar al-Sunna (locally called Al-Shabaab, unrelated to Somali group) seized the port town of Mocímboa da Praia in August 2020. Total SA suspended its $20B LNG project. Rwandan and SADC forces have been deployed.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Europe: loses major potential Russian gas alternative. Total SA: $20B project frozen. Mozambique: loses transformational revenue. South Africa: regional security destabilised. East Africa: insurgency spreading.

slide6.headline: 56 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — energy geopolitics extends to places most people can't find on a map.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Every Ship Entering The Suez Canal Waits At Anchor Here
slide1.body: Port Said is the Mediterranean entrance to the Suez Canal. When the canal is congested or a ship gets stuck, hundreds of vessels anchor here waiting. It's where the queue forms.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Port Said, Egypt — Suez Canal North Entrance
slide2.body: The northern entrance to the Suez Canal on the Mediterranean coast. Ships convoy through in groups — northbound and southbound alternating. Congestion here signals global supply chain stress.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: When The Queue At Port Said Grows, The World Notices.
slide3.body: Ship queues here are a real-time indicator of global trade stress. During Ever Given: 369 ships queued. During Houthi crisis: traffic dropped 40%. Port Said is the intake valve for 15% of world trade.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Gaza Is 70km From Here. Conflict Spillover Is A Real Risk.
slide4.body: The 2023-24 Gaza conflict brought conflict to Egypt's doorstep. Missiles have been intercepted near the canal zone. Egypt is desperately maintaining the canal's neutrality — its revenues depend on it.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Egypt: canal revenues are ~2% of GDP, every disruption costs millions per day. Europe: Mediterranean imports queue up immediately. Shipping companies: demurrage costs for anchored vessels. Global insurance: rates spike on any regional incident.

slide6.headline: 55 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the queue at Port Said is a live feed of global trade health.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Oman's Musandam Peninsula Is An Exclave Completely Surrounded By UAE — And It Controls The Strait
slide1.body: Musandam is a piece of Oman surrounded by UAE territory on land, but its coastline forms the southern shore of the Strait of Hormuz. Without Musandam, no one controls the strait's southern approach.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Musandam Peninsula, Oman
slide2.body: A dramatic fjord landscape on the southern tip of the Hormuz strait. Surrounded by UAE on three land sides but connected to Oman by sea. Oman's most strategically valuable piece of territory.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Oman Is Iran's Back-Channel — And Controls The South Shore Of Hormuz.
slide3.body: Oman maintains diplomatic relations with Iran when no one else will. It mediates. It has hosted US-Iran backchannel talks. While doing so, it sits on the southern shore of the most critical oil chokepoint in the world.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Oman's Balancing Act Between Iran, UAE, Saudi Arabia And The West Is Remarkable And Fragile
slide4.body: Oman is the only Gulf state maintaining full relations with Iran while being a Western partner. When Sultan Qaboos died in 2020, the succession created uncertainty about whether this balancing act would continue.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Global energy: if Oman shifts position, Hormuz's southern shore is no longer neutral. Iran-West diplomacy: loses its main back-channel. UAE: land corridor to Musandam becomes politically complicated. India: major trading partner with Oman.

slide6.headline: 54 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — geopolitics is mostly geography plus centuries of unresolved disputes.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Singapore Handles 37 Million Containers Per Year Through A Strait 1.7km Wide
slide1.body: The Singapore Strait is the exit of the Malacca Strait. One of the world's most trafficked waterways, navigating 1.7km with ships in both directions, every direction, around the clock.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Singapore Strait, Singapore
slide2.body: Between Singapore and Indonesia's Batam and Bintan islands. 1.7km at its narrowest. The world's 2nd busiest port (Singapore) on one shore. ~1,000 ships per day transit these waters.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: ~$600 Billion Of Trade Per Year Through A 1.7km Gap.
slide3.body: Singapore is the world's largest transshipment hub. Every Asian export heading west, every European import heading east, passes through here. Singapore's entire existence depends on keeping this strait open and efficient.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: A Collision In 2017 Killed 10 US Sailors And Closed The Strait For Hours
slide4.body: The USS John S. McCain collision with a merchant vessel killed 10 sailors and briefly disrupted traffic. It revealed how fragile the densely trafficked strait is. One incident can back up hundreds of ships.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Singapore: entire economy at risk. Global shipping: ~$600B in annual trade disrupted. Electronics supply chain: immediate disruption. Energy markets: LNG and oil tankers backed up. Every Asian exporter: delayed shipments.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Supertankers Can't Use Malacca. They Use This Instead.
slide1.body: The Lombok Strait is too deep and too wide for pirates, too deep for mines, and deep enough for the largest VLCCs (Very Large Crude Carriers) that can't transit the shallower Malacca.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Lombok Strait — Deep Water Channel
slide2.body: Southern end of the strait between Bali and Lombok. Maximum depth ~250m — deep enough for fully loaded supertankers that can't use Malacca's shallow sections. A natural deepwater bypass.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Route For VLCCs Too Big For Malacca.
slide3.body: Very Large Crude Carriers from the Middle East to China — carrying up to 3 million barrels — are too big for Malacca. They transit Lombok. ~50 VLCCs per month. Also the US Navy's preferred submarine route.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Indonesia Is Increasingly Uncomfortable With The Traffic It Can't Control
slide4.body: Indonesia has begun asserting more control over its archipelagic waters. As China's navy grows, Indonesia is watching Chinese submarines transiting Lombok — and not always knowing about it in advance.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: China: oil imports from Middle East severely disrupted. Australia: iron ore exports to China affected. US Navy: key submarine transit route compromised. Global VLCCs: no viable alternative deep-water route.

slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some chokepoints exist because of what can physically fit through them.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: During WWII This Was Called 'The Slot' And Thousands Died In It. Now China Has A Security Pact With The Island Nation Controlling It.
slide1.body: New Georgia Sound — 'The Slot' — was the site of some of WWII's most intense naval battles. Today, China signed a security agreement with the Solomon Islands in 2022. The US had a meltdown.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: New Georgia Sound, Solomon Islands
slide2.body: A deep-water channel through the Solomon Islands in the Southwest Pacific. Australia is 1,700km south. Any naval force controlling these islands can project power across key Pacific trade routes.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Australia's Northern Approaches. China Wants A Naval Base Here.
slide3.body: The Solomons sit across Australia's northern sea lanes. A Chinese naval presence here would threaten Australia-US military communications, Pacific trade routes, and the entire US 'second island chain' defence concept.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: China Signed A Security Pact With The Solomons In April 2022. Australia Nearly Had A Diplomatic Incident.
slide4.body: The pact allows Chinese military ships to dock in the Solomons. The Australian PM called it 'the worst security situation since WWII.' The US and Australia are now spending heavily to counter Chinese influence there.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Australia: northern security perimeter compromised. US Pacific strategy: second island chain concept threatened. New Zealand: dependent on Australia's security umbrella. Pacific Island states: increasing great power competition.
