slide6.headline: 51 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — WWII geography is becoming relevant again in the Pacific.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Iraq And Iran Fought An 8-Year War Over This River. It's Still Disputed.
slide1.body: The Shatt al-Arab river forms the Iraq-Iran border for 200km before entering the Persian Gulf. Its exact boundary has caused two wars and is still not fully agreed. Iraq's only sea outlet runs through it.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Shatt al-Arab Waterway, Iraq/Iran
slide2.body: The confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates before entering the Persian Gulf. Forms the Iraq-Iran border. Iraq's only access to the sea. ~2 million barrels of Iraqi oil export per day depends on this waterway.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Iraq's Only Sea Access. 2 Million Barrels Per Day.
slide3.body: Iraq is the world's 5th largest oil exporter. Its oil terminals at Basra handle ~90% of Iraq's export revenue. All of it exits through a waterway disputed with Iran. That's approximately $100M per day of oil through a contested river.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: The Iran-Iraq War (1980-88) Started With A Dispute Over This Waterway
slide4.body: Saddam Hussein tore up the 1975 Algiers Agreement on the Shatt al-Arab boundary in September 1980 and invaded Iran. Eight years, a million dead, no border change. The dispute was never fully resolved.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Iraq: entire export economy depends on these terminals. Global oil market: 2 million barrels per day removed from supply. Iran: reciprocal disruption to Abadan refinery access. Kuwait: regional instability directly threatens its economy.

slide6.headline: 50 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some border disputes are worth a million lives to some governments.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: A Contested Arctic Strait Between Two NATO Allies Nobody Talks About
slide1.body: Nares Strait separates Canada's Ellesmere Island from Greenland (Denmark). Both are NATO allies. Both claim it. As Arctic ice melts and the passage opens, the dispute is becoming more urgent.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Nares Strait, Canadian Arctic
slide2.body: Between Ellesmere Island (Canada) and Greenland (Denmark). 35km wide. Currently iced most of the year, but climate change is opening it. A future submarine and shipping route between the Arctic Ocean and Baffin Bay.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: It Will Be A Major Arctic Shipping Route In 20-30 Years.
slide3.body: Currently blocked by ice most of the year but the window is opening. Arctic submarine operations already use it. Future mineral and energy extraction in the High Arctic will require this route. Sovereignty disputes need to be resolved before traffic arrives.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Denmark Is Spending Massively On Greenland Defence After Trump Said He Wanted To Buy It
slide4.body: Trump's 2019 (and 2025) suggestions about buying Greenland triggered Danish investment in Arctic defence. The strategic value of Nares Strait is part of why. US, Canada and Denmark are all eyeing the same Arctic approaches.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Canada-Denmark relations: sovereignty dispute between allies. US Arctic strategy: complicated by allied dispute. NATO Arctic flank: governance gap in a key defensive zone. Climate vulnerable communities: increased shipping traffic through fragile ecosystem.

slide6.headline: 49 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the Arctic edition is just getting started.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Every Ship From West Africa To Europe Passes Through Waters Controlled By An Island Nation Of 500,000 People
slide1.body: Cape Verde sits in the middle of the North Atlantic shipping lanes between Africa and Europe. Small island nation, enormous strategic position.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Cape Verde, North Atlantic
slide2.body: 570km off Senegal's coast. Right in the middle of transatlantic and Europe-West Africa shipping routes. ~2,000 ships per month transit nearby waters. Major refuelling and resupply hub.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: West Africa's Oil Exports To Europe Transit These Waters.
slide3.body: Nigeria, Angola, Equatorial Guinea — West Africa's major oil exporters. Their tankers pass through Cape Verde's EEZ. Portuguese-speaking, politically stable, strategically placed — Cape Verde punches far above its weight.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Gulf Of Guinea Piracy Peaked In 2020 With 130 Incidents
slide4.body: 2020 was the worst year for piracy globally since 2011 — almost all in the Gulf of Guinea south of Cape Verde. Hostage-taking pirates operate in waters that flow through this passage.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: West African oil exporters: security costs added to every tanker. Europe: West African crude imports affected. NATO Atlantic strategy: Cape Verde's port access matters for naval deployments. Portuguese-speaking world: diplomatic hub.

slide6.headline: 48 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — small islands in big oceans.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Galápagos Of The Indian Ocean Has A UAE Military Base And A Civil War Next Door
slide1.body: Socotra Island has unique biodiversity found nowhere else. It also sits at the mouth of the Gulf of Aden controlling approaches to Bab el-Mandeb. The UAE built a military presence there during Yemen's civil war.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Socotra Island, Yemen
slide2.body: 240km off Yemen's coast, 240km from Somalia. Legally part of Yemen. The UAE has been developing military facilities there since 2018, drawing Yemeni government protests. Strategic position in Gulf of Aden approaches.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Controls The Eastern Approaches To Bab el-Mandeb And Gulf Of Aden.
slide3.body: Any naval force at Socotra commands the approaches from the Arabian Sea into the Gulf of Aden. Combined with a position at Djibouti, you effectively control the entire Horn of Africa maritime approach.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: UAE Deployed Forces To Socotra Without Yemeni Consent During The Civil War
slide4.body: In May 2018, UAE deployed forces to Socotra — part of Yemen — without coordinating with the Yemeni government they are supposed to be supporting. Saudi Arabia eventually mediated a withdrawal. The UAE still has presence there.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Yemen: sovereignty over its own territory undermined. UAE: diplomatically exposed in Yemen coalition. Houthi threat: eastern approach to Gulf of Aden matters for Houthi missile range. Global shipping: alternative to Bab el-Mandeb approaches.

name: Natuna Sea — South China Sea Periphery

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: China Claims Waters Inside Indonesia's Exclusive Economic Zone. Indonesia Disagrees.
slide1.body: China's nine-dash line — its claim to most of the South China Sea — overlaps with Indonesia's Natuna Islands EEZ. Indonesia doesn't claim to be a South China Sea claimant. But China doesn't care.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Natuna Sea, Indonesia
slide2.body: The Natuna Islands sit at the southern edge of the South China Sea. China's nine-dash line extends into what Indonesia considers its exclusive economic zone. Multiple standoffs between Indonesian and Chinese vessels.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Natural Gas Fields Worth Billions Are Under A Disputed EEZ.
slide3.body: Indonesia has major natural gas fields in the Natuna Sea. China's coast guard regularly escorts Chinese fishing vessels into Indonesia's EEZ. Indonesia has deployed military assets to the islands. The gas is the prize.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Indonesia Renamed The Sea 'North Natuna Sea' To Assert Sovereignty. China Ignored It.
slide4.body: In 2017, Indonesia renamed the area on official maps. China simply doesn't acknowledge Indonesian jurisdiction. Indonesian coast guard vessels have repeatedly confronted Chinese coast guard vessels escorting fishing boats.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Indonesia: gas revenues threatened. China: escalation risks in a relationship it values for trade. ASEAN: internal divisions as members have different China stances. US: Indonesia is non-aligned and won't automatically side with Washington.

name: Andaman Sea — Bay of Bengal Gateway

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: India And China Are Building Competing Ports On The Same Sea
slide1.body: The Andaman Sea connects the Bay of Bengal to the Malacca Strait. India has military bases in the Andaman Islands. China is building ports in Myanmar right on its shores. Both know exactly what the other is doing.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Andaman Sea, Bay of Bengal
slide2.body: Between Myanmar, Thailand and India's Andaman Islands. The approach to the Malacca Strait from the Indian Ocean. India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands straddle this passage with a major tri-services military base.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: India Can Threaten Malacca From Here. China Is Trying To Prevent That.
slide3.body: India's Andaman base gives it the ability to block Chinese ships entering the Malacca Strait. This is China's greatest maritime fear — the 'Malacca Dilemma'. China's String of Pearls strategy in Myanmar is a direct response.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: China Is Building Kyaukpyu Port In Myanmar — 350km From India's Andaman Base
slide4.body: China's $1.3B Kyaukpyu deep-sea port in Myanmar sits 350km from India's main Andaman base. A pipeline already runs from there to Yunnan, China. India has responded by upgrading its military presence significantly.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: China: Malacca blockade scenario becomes viable. India: must maintain expensive military presence. Myanmar: caught between two powers, its territory increasingly contested. ASEAN: regional stability undermined.

slide6.headline: 45 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — India vs China is playing out one port at a time.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Australia's Northern Gateway. China Is Interested. Australia Is Not Happy About That.
slide1.body: The passage between the Indonesian islands and Australia through the Timor Sea is Australia's main northern maritime approach. Chinese naval vessels have been conducting exercises in Australian waters.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Timor Gap, Indonesia/Australia
slide2.body: The maritime boundary between Indonesia and Australia through the Timor Sea. Darwin — Australia's northern gateway — sits 500km south. ~40% of Australia's maritime trade transits nearby waters.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Australia's Northern Approaches Are Its Strategic Vulnerability.
slide3.body: Australia is a maritime nation with a small population defending a vast coastline. The Timor Gap is where it's most exposed. LNG exports from Darwin. Military supplies from the north. Any adversary wanting to threaten Australia starts here.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Chinese Naval Vessels Conducted Exercises In The Arafura Sea In 2023
slide4.body: In February 2023, Chinese navy vessels conducted exercises in the Arafura Sea between Australia and New Guinea. Australia detected them and tracked them. This was the closest Chinese naval activity to Australian territory in decades.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Australia: northern exposure increases defence costs dramatically. East Timor: sitting between the two powers, dependent on Australian security. Indonesia: non-aligned position becomes harder to maintain. AUKUS: entire rationale is this passage.

name: Gulf of Mexico — Yucatan to Florida

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Gulf Of Mexico Is A Contained Sea With Two Exits. Both Are Chokepoints.
slide1.body: The Gulf of Mexico is nearly landlocked. All trade exits through the Yucatán Channel (west) or Florida Strait (east). Houston — the US's largest port by tonnage — sits inside this enclosed sea.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Gulf of Mexico, North America
slide2.body: Nearly enclosed by the US, Mexico and Cuba. Two exits: Yucatán Channel and Florida Strait. Hosts the world's 4th largest offshore oil production. Home to the US's largest port complex.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: ~2 Million Barrels Of US Gulf Coast Oil Per Day. Plus US LNG Export Terminal Hub.
slide3.body: US Gulf offshore produces ~2M bpd. Major LNG export terminals: Sabine Pass, Cameron, Corpus Christi. All exits through two chokepoints. The Gulf is the engine of US energy exports — trapped inside a near-landlocked sea.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Hurricane Katrina Disrupted Gulf Energy Infrastructure For 6 Months
slide4.body: 2005's Hurricane Katrina shut down Gulf platforms and pipelines for months. 2021's Hurricane Ida cut ~95% of Gulf oil production briefly. Climate change is making Gulf hurricanes stronger and more frequent.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US energy exports: immediate disruption. Europe: LNG imports from US stopped. US Gulf Coast communities: energy and employment crisis. Global LNG market: significant supply shock. Caribbean energy-dependent nations: cut off.

slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some chokepoints are weather-dependent. The Gulf's are increasingly so.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: One Of The World's Most Shallow And Dangerous Shipping Channels Has No Viable Alternative
slide1.body: Torres Strait connects the Coral Sea and the Arafura Sea. It's shallow, reef-dotted, and requires a pilot. Large ships can't use it. But for smaller vessels connecting Australia's east and west coasts, it's essential.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Torres Strait, Australia/PNG
slide2.body: Between Cape York (Australia) and Papua New Guinea. 150km wide but shallow and reef-hazardous. Requires mandatory pilotage for vessels over 70m. Alternative requires going around Australia — adding 5,000km.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Shortcut Between Australia's East And West Coasts. For Ships That Can Fit.
slide3.body: Bulk carriers carrying iron ore or coal can't use Torres Strait due to depth. But smaller cargo vessels, fishing fleets, and supply ships for Queensland and Northern Territory depend on it. PNG trade runs through it.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Climate Change Is Threatening To Make Torres Strait Islands Uninhabitable Within Decades
slide4.body: The Torres Strait Islands sit at ~3m elevation. Sea level rise is already affecting them. In 2022, the UN Human Rights Committee ruled Australia had violated the rights of Torres Strait Islanders by inadequate climate action.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Torres Strait Islander communities: homes underwater. PNG: trade route affected. Australian coastal shipping: loses the east-west shortcut. Queensland ports: increased transit costs. Coral Sea fisheries: ecosystem disruption.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Somali Pirates Cost Global Shipping $18 Billion In One Year. Then Navies Arrived.
slide1.body: At their peak in 2011, Somali pirates were attacking ~150 ships per year and holding hundreds of hostages. The economic impact reached $18 billion in a single year. Then every major navy sent warships. Pirates retreated. Now Houthis took over the same corridor.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Gulf of Aden, Somalia/Yemen
slide2.body: Between Somalia and Yemen. The approach to Bab el-Mandeb. ~20,000 ships per year. At peak piracy 2008-2011: ~600 sailors held hostage at once. Multi-national naval force (CMF) has patrolled since 2008.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Approach To Bab el-Mandeb. Currently The World's Most Dangerous Shipping Corridor.
slide3.body: In 2023-24, Houthi attacks replaced Somali piracy as the main threat. The same corridor. The same ships. Different attackers with missiles and drones instead of speedboats and AK-47s. The economics of disruption are the same.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Houthis Have Attacked 100+ Ships. Multiple Have Sunk Or Been Abandoned.
slide4.body: Since October 2023, Houthi attacks have made the Gulf of Aden a war zone. The Galaxy Leader vessel was seized with its entire crew. Multiple ships have been abandoned. US-UK strikes on Yemen have not stopped the attacks.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Global shipping: freight rates doubled. Egypt: Suez revenues cut 40%. Regional ports: Djibouti handling overflow. Sailors: direct physical danger. Global consumers: higher prices on everything from Asia.

slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the Gulf of Aden has been a war zone for most of the last 20 years.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Spice Islands Controlled The World's Economy For 300 Years. The Sea Around Them Still Matters.
slide1.body: The Banda Sea was the centre of the global spice trade — nutmeg and cloves worth their weight in gold. The Dutch killed for it. The British schemed for it. Today it's a critical submarine transit zone.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Banda Sea, Indonesia
slide2.body: Deep, enclosed sea in eastern Indonesia surrounded by the Maluku (Spice) Islands. Maximum depth 7,440m. Used by nuclear submarines for deep-water transit. Historically the most fought-over maritime zone in Asia.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Deep Enough For Submarines To Hide. Strategic Enough For Everyone To Want Access.
slide3.body: The Banda Sea is one of the deepest seas in the world — ideal for submarine operations. US and Australian submarines transit it. Indonesia doesn't always know when. Its central position between Pacific and Indian Ocean routes makes it irreplaceable.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Indonesia Faces Chinese, US And Australian Submarines In Its Waters Simultaneously
slide4.body: Indonesia's archipelagic waters are transited by submarines from three different powers — China, the US, and soon Australia (AUKUS). Indonesia's official policy is that all must notify and request permission. In practice, they don't.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Indonesia: sovereignty increasingly notional in its own waters. Australia: AUKUS submarines depend on this zone for Indo-Pacific reach. US: loses quiet submarine access if Indonesia asserts rights. Regional stability: three-power submarine competition.

slide6.headline: 40 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the Spice Islands were the original globalisation chokepoint.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Landlocked Malawi's Only Access To The Sea Runs Through Mozambique's Most Unstable Province
slide1.body: The Nacala Corridor connects Mozambique's port to Malawi and Zambia. Brazil's Vale has invested billions in a railway. And the route runs through a province dealing with an Islamist insurgency.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Nacala Port, Northern Mozambique
slide2.body: One of East Africa's deepest natural harbours. Gateway for landlocked Malawi and parts of Zambia. Vale (Brazil) and other mining companies export coal and minerals through here. The corridor runs 912km inland.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Landlocked Countries' Only Export Route. 18 Million People Depend On This Port.
slide3.body: Malawi (20 million people) has no coastline. Nacala is its closest port access. Vale's Mozambique coal exports (halted) were worth $4B/year. Japan helped fund the corridor railway. The port handles East Africa's emerging economy.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Insurgents Have Attacked Railway Infrastructure Serving The Corridor
slide4.body: The same Cabo Delgado insurgency threatening LNG projects has attacked infrastructure in northern Mozambique. Railway sabotage, attacks on towns along the corridor. Vale had to halt coal production citing security.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Malawi: import and export costs skyrocket. Vale: billions in investment frozen. Japan: development finance returns. East African integration: regional trade corridors collapse. Mining companies: force majeure declared.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The World's Largest Lake Has 50 Billion Barrels Of Oil Beneath It And No Way Out To Sea
slide1.body: The Caspian Sea is an enclosed body of water. The oil and gas beneath it — among the world's largest reserves — can only leave by pipeline. Every pipeline crosses one of five countries. All of them have complicated relationships with each other.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Caspian Sea, Central Asia
slide2.body: Enclosed sea between Russia, Iran, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan. ~50 billion barrels of oil reserves. No ocean access — everything must leave by pipeline or rail. A geopolitical pressure cooker.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan And Turkmenistan's Entire Economies Depend On Getting Oil Out.
slide3.body: Kazakhstan alone has ~30B barrels of oil. The main pipeline (CPC) goes through Russia to the Black Sea. After Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Western countries scrambled to find alternative routes — all crossing complicated territory.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Russia Damaged The CPC Pipeline To Pressure Kazakhstan After Ukraine Sanctions
slide4.body: In 2022, Russia announced 'inspections' that shut the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) — Kazakhstan's main oil export route — for 30 days. It was widely seen as retaliation for Kazakhstan's neutral stance on Ukraine. Kazakhstan's economy lost ~$1B.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Kazakhstan: entire oil economy hostage to Russia's mood. Azerbaijan: BTC pipeline to Turkey creates an alternative but Russia resents it. Turkmenistan: most trapped, options most limited. Europe: desperately wanted Caspian gas as Russia alternative.

slide6.headline: 38 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — the world's largest lake is a geopolitical trap.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: India Threatened To Stop Pakistan's River Water. Pakistan Said That Would Be An Act Of War.
slide1.body: The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 divides the Indus river system between India and Pakistan. India has threatened to 'review' it after terrorist attacks. Pakistan called any change an act of war. 200 million people drink this water.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Indus River System, Pakistan/India
slide2.body: The Indus flows from Tibet through India-administered Kashmir and then through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea. Six rivers, one treaty from 1960, two nuclear-armed states. Pakistan gets the western rivers; India the eastern.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Pakistan's Agriculture Depends 90% On Indus Water. India Controls The Upstream.
slide3.body: Pakistan is one of the world's most water-stressed countries. ~90% of agriculture depends on the Indus system. India is upstream. The Indus Waters Treaty has survived three wars — but in an era of climate change and rising nationalism, its survival is not guaranteed.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: India Formally Notified Pakistan Of Intent To 'Review' The Treaty In 2023
slide4.body: Following Kashmiri militant attacks, India sent Pakistan a formal notice in 2023 seeking to modify the Indus Waters Treaty. Pakistan's government called it an 'illegal and unilateral' act and a 'hostile move'. Both sides have nuclear weapons.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Pakistan: agricultural catastrophe, food insecurity for 220 million. India: diplomatic isolation, escalation with nuclear-armed neighbour. Afghanistan: upstream changes affect Kabul River flows. South Asia: water conflict becomes most destabilising factor.

slide6.headline: 37 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — water is the next resource wars will be fought over. They're already starting.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Every Invader Of India Came Through Here. Alexander The Great. The Mughals. The British. The US Didn't.
slide1.body: The Khyber Pass has been the main land route between Central Asia and the Indian Subcontinent for 2,500 years. Every great conqueror used it. The Americans went through it to supply Afghanistan — until they couldn't.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Khyber Pass, Pakistan/Afghanistan
slide2.body: 53km long mountain pass at 1,070m. Connects Peshawar (Pakistan) to Jalalabad (Afghanistan). Main land crossing between the two countries. Alexander used it. The British Empire maintained it at great cost. The US tried.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Afghanistan Has No Coastline. Everything Goes Through Pakistan Via This Pass.
slide3.body: Afghanistan is landlocked. The Khyber Pass is its main connection to Pakistan's ports. ~70% of NATO supplies to Afghanistan went through this route during the 2001-2021 war. Pakistan's ability to close it gave it enormous leverage over the US.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Pakistan Closed The Khyber Pass To NATO Supplies For 7 Months In 2011-12
slide4.body: After a US airstrike killed 24 Pakistani soldiers in November 2011, Pakistan shut the Khyber Pass to NATO supply convoys. For 7 months. The US had to reroute through Russia and Central Asia at much higher cost.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Afghanistan: cut off from sea access. Pakistan: leverage over neighbours but economic damage from instability. Trade: Central Asia-South Asia trade corridor disrupted. US military: lessons about supply line vulnerability.

slide6.headline: 36 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — mountain passes are chokepoints too. Ask Alexander.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Iran Occupied Three UAE Islands In 1971. Still Hasn't Left. The Islands Command The Strait Of Hormuz.
slide1.body: Three small islands — Abu Musa and the Tunbs — sit in the middle of the Strait of Hormuz. The UAE claims them. Iran occupies them. From these islands, you can command the entire strait.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Abu Musa Island, Persian Gulf
slide2.body: A small island 70km from Dubai, sitting in the western approach to the Strait of Hormuz. Iran seized it from the UAE (then Sharjah) in 1971, one day before British withdrawal. Has been occupied ever since.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Iran Has Military Installations On An Island Commanding The World's Oil Artery.
slide3.body: Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunb islands give Iran direct observation and potential control over the Strait of Hormuz western approaches. Radar stations, military garrison. The UAE considers this Iranian occupation of sovereign Emirati territory.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Iran Reinforced The Islands In 1992 And Has Been Expanding Installations Ever Since
slide4.body: In 1992, Iran unilaterally extended its control of Abu Musa, expelling UAE residents. Since then, it has expanded military facilities, built an airstrip, and positioned weapons. Every Arab League summit since has called for Iranian withdrawal.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: UAE: sovereign territory occupied. Arab states: precedent for Iranian territorial expansion. Global energy: islands provide Iran with chokepoint military assets. Abraham Accords: UAE-Israel normalisation partly motivated by shared Iran concerns.

slide6.headline: 35 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Iran has been playing the long game in the Persian Gulf for 50 years.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Seattle And Vancouver's Port Access Runs Through 25km Of Jointly Controlled Waters
slide1.body: The Strait of Juan de Fuca is the only entrance to Puget Sound (Seattle) and the Strait of Georgia (Vancouver). Every container ship, tanker, and cruise ship for two of North America's largest ports squeezes through here.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Juan de Fuca, USA/Canada
slide2.body: 160km long, 25km wide. US-Canada border runs down the middle. Access to Seattle's ports, Vancouver's ports, and numerous military facilities including Bangor submarine base — home to 8 Ohio-class submarines.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: 8 US Nuclear Submarines Base Here. So Does Pacific Northwest Trade.
slide3.body: Naval Station Bangor on Puget Sound is home to 8 Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines — about 1/3 of the US nuclear deterrent at sea. Every sub deployment and return transits Juan de Fuca. Plus ~$100B in annual trade.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: A Major Earthquake Here — The Cascadia Subduction Zone — Could Trigger A Tsunami In The Strait
slide4.body: The Cascadia Subduction Zone offshore will produce a magnitude 9+ earthquake — scientists say it's a matter of when, not if. A 2016 FEMA exercise projected 13,000 deaths. The strait would be physically damaged for months.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US nuclear deterrent: submarine base inaccessible. Seattle and Vancouver ports: trade paralysed. Pacific Northwest economy: $300B+ GDP disrupted. US military: Ohio-class submarines unable to deploy from primary base.

slide6.headline: 34 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — some chokepoints are also nuclear submarine highways.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Russia's Second City Has Only One Route To The Baltic. And Now Both Shores Are NATO.
slide1.body: St Petersburg — Russia's main Baltic port — can only be reached through the Gulf of Finland. Since Finland joined NATO in 2023, both shores of the entrance are now NATO territory. Russia is boxed in.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Gulf of Finland Entrance, Baltic Sea
slide2.body: The narrow entrance to the Gulf of Finland between Finland and Estonia. Both countries joined NATO in 2023-24. St Petersburg — Russia's second city and main Baltic port — can only be reached through this gap.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Russia's Baltic Fleet And St Petersburg Are Now Surrounded By NATO.
slide3.body: Finland's NATO membership means Russia's entire Baltic coast is now flanked by NATO members on both sides. The Gulf of Finland is a NATO-controlled bottleneck. Russia's Baltic trade and naval access has never been more constrained.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Russia Declared Finland An 'Unfriendly State' Immediately After Its NATO Application
slide4.body: Russia responded to Finland's NATO application with threats and the declaration of 'unfriendly state' status. The Finnish-Russian border — 1,340km, the longest EU-Russia border — is now a NATO frontier. Tensions are highest since the Cold War.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Russia: Baltic naval access severely constrained. St Petersburg: trade costs increase. Finland: Russia has cut all energy supplies and created economic friction. Estonia: front-line NATO state facing Russian pressure. Baltic Sea: fully NATO lake.

slide6.headline: 33 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Finland joining NATO changed the entire Baltic geography overnight.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Myanmar's Military Junta Controls The Only Exit For A Country China Needs As A Sea Bypass
slide1.body: The Irrawaddy River is Myanmar's economic artery. Its delta and Yangon port are the country's gateway. China has invested billions in a pipeline from the coast to Yunnan — bypassing the Malacca Strait. The military junta controls all of it.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Irrawaddy Delta, Myanmar
slide2.body: Myanmar's main river system emptying into the Andaman Sea near Yangon. China's Myanmar-Yunnan pipeline — a strategic Malacca bypass — runs through here. The 2021 military coup disrupted all investment.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: China's Most Important Malacca Bypass Runs Through A Country In Civil War.
slide3.body: China has invested ~$3B in a port and pipeline from Kyaukpyu through Myanmar to Yunnan. If completed, it allows oil tankers to dock in Myanmar and pump oil directly to China — bypassing Malacca entirely. The 2021 coup froze everything.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Myanmar Has Been In Civil War Since 2021. China's Pipeline Is Running Through A Warzone.
slide4.body: After the February 2021 coup, Myanmar descended into multi-front civil war. Resistance forces control large territories. Chinese pipeline infrastructure has been attacked. China is trying to maintain relations with the junta while its investments burn.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: China: Malacca bypass strategy set back by years. Myanmar people: civilian catastrophe, millions displaced. Regional trade: ASEAN corridor disrupted. India: Chinese port next door raises security concerns. ASEAN: member state in civil war.

slide6.headline: 32 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — geopolitical investments in unstable countries tend to go badly.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Every Tanker That Exits Hormuz Has To Transit These Waters On Both Sides
slide1.body: Ships entering and exiting the Strait of Hormuz must pass through the Gulf of Oman. It's the second half of the chokepoint — and where Iran has been most aggressive in seizing and harassing vessels.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Gulf of Oman
slide2.body: Between Oman, Iran and Pakistan. The staging area for Hormuz transits. Ships slow here to navigate Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guard speedboat bases are on the northern shore. ~20 million barrels of oil transits daily.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Every Hormuz Transit Starts And Ends Here. It's Where Iran Operates.
slide3.body: Ships can't enter or exit Hormuz without transiting the Gulf of Oman. This is where Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy operates most aggressively. Limpet mine attacks in 2019. Tanker seizures in 2019 and 2023. The entire strait system has two chokepoints.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Iran Attacked Six Tankers In The Gulf Of Oman With Limpet Mines In 2019
slide4.body: June 2019: Iran attacked two tankers in the Gulf of Oman — Japanese-owned, Norwegian-operated. May 2019: four tankers attacked off Fujairah. The US military showed video of Iranian forces removing an unexploded mine. Iran denied everything.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Global oil: insurance costs for Gulf tankers doubled overnight. Japan: tankers attacked while PM Abe was in Tehran trying to mediate. Oman: caught between Iranian and Western pressure. Shipping companies: operational costs spike.

slide6.headline: 31 More Chokepoints.
slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Iran treats the Gulf of Oman as its operational backyard.

name: Red Sea — Northern Approach / Gulf of Suez

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Everything Heading To The Suez Canal First Has To Fit Through Here
slide1.body: The Gulf of Suez is the northern Red Sea — the 300km approach to the Suez Canal entrance. Egypt controls both shores. It's the funnel that feeds the world's most important artificial waterway.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Gulf of Suez, Egypt
slide2.body: Between the Sinai Peninsula and the Egyptian mainland. 300km long, 30km wide. The mandatory approach route to the Suez Canal. ~50 ships per day transit. Egypt's offshore oil fields are here.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Suez Canal Has No Value Without A Clear Approach. This Is The Approach.
slide3.body: Suez Canal capacity is 86 ships per day. All of them approach through the Gulf of Suez from the south. Egypt's Sinai Peninsula flanks the eastern shore — historically a conflict zone. Any disruption here stacks up hundreds of ships.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: ISIS Attacked Egyptian Military Convoys In Sinai Repeatedly From 2013-2020
slide4.body: Wilayat Sinai (ISIS affiliate) conducted sustained attacks on Egyptian forces in northern Sinai for years. The Sinai Peninsula forms the eastern shore of the Gulf of Suez — ISIS was active on the shore of a major shipping approach.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Egypt: canal revenues at risk. Global shipping: Suez approach disrupted. Saudi Arabia: northern Red Sea energy flows affected. Israel: Eilat port access via Red Sea complicated. European importers: supply chains immediately affected.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Zimbabwe Has No Coast. Its Lifeline Goes Through A Mozambican Port That A Cyclone Just Destroyed.
slide1.body: The Beira Corridor is Zimbabwe, Zambia and Malawi's main access to the sea. In March 2019, Cyclone Idai made direct landfall on Beira — destroying port infrastructure and the entire corridor. Landlocked countries were stranded.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Beira Port, Mozambique
slide2.body: Mozambique's second-largest port. Serves Zimbabwe, Zambia, and parts of Malawi. The corridor railway and road system runs 600km inland. Cyclone Idai in 2019 devastated the port and surrounding infrastructure.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Three Landlocked Countries Depend On One Port In A Cyclone Zone.
slide3.body: Zimbabwe imports and exports through Beira. Zambia's copper exports — ~$7B/year — partially route through here. When Cyclone Idai struck, landlocked countries had to urgently reroute through South Africa at much higher cost.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Climate Change Is Making Cyclones In The Mozambique Channel Stronger And More Frequent
slide4.body: Idai 2019, Kenneth 2019 (same year, second major cyclone), Eloise 2021, Ana 2022, Freddy 2023. The southern Mozambique Channel is seeing increasing cyclone activity. The port is in the direct path of intensifying storms.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Zimbabwe: import and export costs spike immediately. Zambia: copper export revenues lost. Regional food security: landlocked countries' food imports disrupted. Development finance: infrastructure investment deterred by climate risk.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Japan Attacked Hawaii To Control The Pacific. China's Military Is Studying The Same Geometry.
slide1.body: Pearl Harbor was attacked because Hawaii controls the Central Pacific. US Pacific Command is still based there. Every US military response in the Pacific flows through Hawaii. China's military planners know this.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Hawaii, Central Pacific
slide2.body: US Pacific Command headquarters. Home to 50,000+ military personnel. Equidistant between the US mainland and Asia. The hub for all US Pacific military operations. An attack on Hawaii would cripple US Pacific strategy.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Every US Aircraft Carrier Deployment In The Pacific Is Coordinated From Here.
slide3.body: INDOPACOM — the largest US regional command — runs from Pearl Harbor. All carrier group deployments, submarine operations, logistics. In 2023, the US invested $22B in Hawaii military infrastructure, the largest peacetime military build in the Pacific.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: China's DF-41 ICBM Can Hit Hawaii In 30 Minutes. So Can North Korea's Missiles.
slide4.body: Hawaii is within range of Chinese ICBMs and North Korean ballistic missiles. In January 2018, Hawaii issued an emergency ballistic missile alert (false alarm) that caused mass panic. The threat is real and acknowledged.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US Pacific strategy: command hub destroyed. Japan and South Korea: lose primary US military coordination. Australia and Philippines: US alliances immediately weakened. Global power balance: most significant shift since WWII.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Russia's Main Pacific Port Freezes In Winter And Can Only Be Reached Through Other Countries' Waters
slide1.body: Vladivostok is Russia's primary Pacific city and naval base. To reach the open Pacific, Russian ships must transit through waters near Japan or Korea. Russia does not control a single exit from its own backyard.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Vladivostok, Russian Far East
slide2.body: Russia's largest Pacific port. Home to the Russian Pacific Fleet. Exits require transiting Tsugaru Strait (Japan), Korea Strait (Korea/Japan), or La Pérouse Strait (Japan). Russia is geographically bottled up in its own Pacific.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Russia's Pacific Fleet Cannot Reach The Pacific Without Japan's Cooperation.
slide3.body: Every exit from Vladivostok runs near Japanese or Korean territory. Japan could effectively block the Russian Pacific Fleet from the open ocean in a conflict scenario. This is why Russia is so sensitive about Japanese sovereignty disputes over the Kuril Islands.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Russia Gave China Vladivostok Port Access In 2023 As Russia's Pacific Fleet Deteriorates
slide4.body: In 2023, Russia granted China transit rights through Vladivostok for river-borne grain trade. Russia's Pacific Fleet has shrunk significantly due to Ukraine war losses and sanctions. China is quietly filling the power vacuum.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Russia: Pacific naval power severely degraded. Japan: Kuril dispute creates constant tension. China: opportunity to increase influence in Russian Far East. South Korea: Russian Pacific Fleet behaviour affects Korean security. US: Pacific balance shifting.

slide6.body: Follow @straitsandcanals — Russia's geography is its biggest strategic problem.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Russia's Safest Nuclear Submarine Patrol Area Is Locked Behind A Japanese Strait
slide1.body: The Sea of Okhotsk — where Russia's ballistic missile submarines hide — can only be entered through straits near Japan. Russia calls it the 'Bastion'. Japan controls the entrance. The Cold War never fully ended here.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: La Pérouse Strait, Russia/Japan
slide2.body: Between Russia's Sakhalin Island and Japan's Hokkaido. 44km wide. One of three exits from the Sea of Japan. Russia's nuclear submarine patrols in the Sea of Okhotsk depend on transiting near Japanese waters.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Russia's Nuclear Deterrent Patrol Area Requires Transiting Japan's Backyard.
slide3.body: Russia's Delta IV submarines patrol the Sea of Okhotsk — protected by shallow waters and Russian anti-submarine forces. To get there from Vladivostok, they must transit La Pérouse or Tsugaru straits. Japan monitors every single passage.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Japan And Russia Have A Disputed Island Chain Right Next Door — Unresolved Since 1945
slide4.body: The Kuril Islands — seized by the USSR in 1945 — are Japan's Northern Territories dispute. Russia and Japan have never signed a peace treaty. The disputed islands dominate the northern approach to these straits. An 80-year-old dispute still affects nuclear submarine routing.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Russia: nuclear submarine operations constrained. Japan: frozen peace treaty with Russia limits options. Regional stability: unresolved WWII dispute creating ongoing friction. US-Japan alliance: Japanese intelligence on Russian submarines is valuable.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: US Submarines Leave The Atlantic For The Caribbean Through Here
slide1.body: The Mona Passage between Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic is the main deep-water route between the Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea for US military vessels. Drug traffickers know it too.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Mona Passage, Puerto Rico/Dominican Republic
slide2.body: 130km wide between Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic. Deep-water access to the Caribbean from the Atlantic. US Eastern Seaboard's naval gateway to the Caribbean. Primary drug trafficking route from South America.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: US Navy's Atlantic-Caribbean Gateway. Also Drug Trafficking Highway.
slide3.body: Every US carrier group moving from Norfolk to the Caribbean passes through Mona Passage. Simultaneously, DEA estimates significant cocaine trafficking through these waters. The US tries to do both — military transit and interdiction — at the same time.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Venezuela Has Claimed Waters Near Here And Periodically Harasses US Vessels
slide4.body: Venezuela under Maduro has had multiple confrontations with US naval and Coast Guard vessels in Caribbean waters. With Russia maintaining a military presence in Venezuela, the eastern Caribbean is more contested than it's been since the Cold War.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US Caribbean operations: disrupted. Puerto Rico: dependent on sea access. Dominican Republic: caught between powers. Drug trafficking: US interdiction efforts affected. Regional stability: US-Venezuela tensions spill into shipping lanes.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: New Zealand's Two Islands Are Connected By The World's Most Unpredictable Ferry Service
slide1.body: Cook Strait divides New Zealand's North and South Islands. It's one of the most treacherous stretches of water in the world. The Interislander ferry is the only land-link. When it stops, New Zealand is effectively two countries.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Cook Strait, New Zealand
slide2.body: 22km at its narrowest between Wellington and Picton. One of the world's most treacherous channels due to strong tidal currents and unpredictable winds. The MV Wahine sank here in 1968 killing 51 people.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The North Island Has 75% Of NZ's Population. The South Has Most Of Its Agriculture.
slide3.body: New Zealand's domestic economy depends on Cook Strait for food and goods movement between islands. Rail freight, trucks, passengers — all on the Interislander ferry. The South Island's dairy and agricultural exports flow to the North Island's ports.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: A Wellington Fault Earthquake Could Close The Strait's Ports And Sink The Ferries
slide4.body: Wellington sits on one of the most dangerous fault lines in New Zealand. A major earthquake (overdue, say geologists) could damage ferry terminals on both shores and trigger landslides into the strait. New Zealand's internal connectivity would be severed.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: New Zealand: economic isolation of entire southern island. Wellington: capital city access to South Island cut. South Island agriculture: export bottleneck. Domestic supply chains: immediate goods shortages in both islands.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Gap Between America And Russia Is 85km. There's A US Island And A Russian Island 4km Apart In The Middle.
slide1.body: The Bering Strait is the only connection between the Arctic and Pacific Oceans. Russia and the US are separated by 85km. The Diomede Islands in the middle are 4km apart — one American, one Russian. The international date line runs between them.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Bering Strait, Alaska/Russia
slide2.body: 85km wide. The Arctic Ocean meets the Pacific. The Diomede Islands split it. Already partially navigable year-round due to climate change. The gateway for everything transiting between the Arctic and Pacific.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: As Arctic Ice Melts, This Becomes One Of The Most Strategic Straits On Earth.
slide3.body: Currently used mainly by fishing and research vessels. But as the Arctic opens, all Arctic shipping — Northern Sea Route, Northwest Passage — must pass through or near the Bering Strait. Russia and the US both know what's coming.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Russia Increased Military Activity In Alaska's Airspace And Waters In 2022-2024
slide4.body: Russian military aircraft have increasingly tested US air defences in Alaska's Air Defense Identification Zone. Russian submarines have been detected near Alaska. The Bering Strait is increasingly a military frontier.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US: northern maritime defence increasingly expensive. Russia: Arctic ambitions require Bering Strait access. Global shipping: future Arctic route governance undecided. Indigenous communities: militarisation of their traditional waters. Climate: increasing traffic in fragile ecosystem.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Italy And France Both Say This Strait Is Dangerous For Tankers. Tankers Keep Using It Anyway.
slide1.body: The Strait of Bonifacio between Corsica (France) and Sardinia (Italy) is officially discouraged for large tanker traffic due to the rocky, current-riddled waters. Ships use it anyway because it saves time.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Bonifacio, France/Italy
slide2.body: 11km wide between Corsica and Sardinia. Rocky seabed, strong currents, challenging navigation. France and Italy tried to ban tanker traffic after multiple incidents. IMO compromise — precautionary area, not banned.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Shortcut Between Western Mediterranean And Tyrrhenian Sea. Worth The Risk.
slide3.body: Ships save significant sailing time using the strait instead of going around Sardinia. That adds up to millions in fuel per voyage. So ships take the risk, despite the currents, rocks and France and Italy's objections.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Multiple Tanker Incidents Including A Greek Tanker Running Aground With 700 Tons Of Fuel Aboard
slide4.body: Several tanker groundings and near-misses in this strait. A Greek tanker carrying 700 tons of diesel ran aground in 2019. The Bonifacio Islands are a UNESCO World Heritage site — an environmental disaster from a tanker spill would be catastrophic.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Corsica and Sardinia: environmental disaster risk. Mediterranean tourism: catastrophic if major spill. France-Italy: diplomatic fallout over tanker traffic they both oppose but can't stop. Shipping industry: route continues despite risks.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: The Great Lakes Are Landlocked Without This Canal. And It's Operated By One Country.
slide1.body: The Welland Canal bypasses Niagara Falls, connecting Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. Without it, the Great Lakes — and all the industry around them — are cut off from the St Lawrence Seaway and the Atlantic. Canada operates it.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Welland Canal, Ontario, Canada
slide2.body: 43km canal between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. 8 locks. Bypasses Niagara Falls. Connects to the St Lawrence Seaway and the Atlantic. Over 40 million tonnes of cargo per year. Canada controls it entirely.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Detroit's Steel. Chicago's Grain. Cleveland's Shipping. All Depend On This Canal.
slide3.body: ~40 million tonnes of US agricultural exports, steel, manufactured goods move through this canal. If it closes, the entire Great Lakes industrial heartland — a significant chunk of US-Canada manufacturing — loses its maritime exit.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: A Ship Got Stuck In 2021. Traffic Backed Up For Days.
slide4.body: A grounded vessel in 2021 backed up traffic for several days — small-scale but demonstrating the bottleneck effect. The locks are aging infrastructure. Any major accident or weather event creates immediate knock-on effects.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: US Midwest agriculture: grain export bottleneck immediate. Great Lakes steel: production delays. Canadian industry: St Lawrence Seaway access lost. Both economies: billions in trade disrupted within days.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: Europe's Inland Waterway Highway Has A Natural Bottleneck Romania And Serbia Share
slide1.body: The Danube is Europe's most important inland waterway — connecting Germany to the Black Sea. The Iron Gates gorge between Romania and Serbia is its most treacherous section. A joint dam controls the flow.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Iron Gates, Romania/Serbia
slide2.body: The Danube gorge on the Romania-Serbia border. A joint hydroelectric dam controls water levels. 2,000km of European inland shipping depends on this section. Grain, oil, and manufactured goods all transit.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: Central Europe's Inland Trade Highway. Grain Out. Fuel In.
slide3.body: ~100 million tonnes per year on the Danube system. Ukrainian grain (before the war), Romanian agriculture, Serbian goods, Hungarian manufactured products. The Iron Gates section is the narrowest point — a bottleneck for all of central European river trade.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Low Water Levels In 2022 Stranded Hundreds Of Ships In The Section
slide4.body: Drought in 2022 dropped Danube water levels to record lows in the Iron Gates section. Ships ran aground. Hundreds were stranded or had to reduce cargo weight. Climate change is making this more frequent.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Romanian agriculture: export corridor disrupted. Serbia: trade bottleneck. Hungary: energy imports affected. Black Sea ports: reduced throughput. Ukrainian grain: alternative export route compromised during Russia's Black Sea blockade.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: 21 Million Barrels A Day In A 3km Lane. Both Ways.
slide1.body: Ships in the Strait of Hormuz travel in designated lanes — 3km wide each way, with a 3km separation zone. Inbound and outbound supertankers pass within 3km of each other through Iranian and Omani territorial waters simultaneously.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Tanker Lanes, Strait of Hormuz
slide2.body: The navigable portion of the strait uses Traffic Separation Schemes — two 3km lanes separated by a 3km buffer. Ships must use these lanes. They pass directly through waters Iran claims as territorial sea.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Lanes Run Through Iranian Territorial Waters. Iran Claims The Right To Inspect Any Ship.
slide3.body: Under UNCLOS, Iran has the right to regulate — though not ban — innocent passage through its territorial waters. It uses this to claim the ability to board and inspect ships. The US 5th Fleet disputes this interpretation. Standoffs are regular.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Iran's IRGCN Has 1,500+ Vessels Including Armed Speedboats Permanently In These Waters
slide4.body: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy maintains a permanent armed presence in the strait. Armed speedboats, submarines, shore-based missiles. This is the most heavily armed maritime chokepoint in the world.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: Global oil market: immediate price spike on any incident. Japan and South Korea: energy emergency within days. India: petrol prices spike within hours. Shipping companies: insurance costs for Gulf voyages surge. World economy: ~$1 per barrel per week of crisis.

slide1.label: CHOKEPOINT
slide1.headline: One Country Owns Both Shores Of The World's Southernmost Commercial Shipping Route
slide1.body: Chile uniquely controls both shores of the Magellan Strait — the only country to have both coasts of a major international strait. It can technically close it. It never has. But it could.

slide2.label: WHERE IT IS
slide2.headline: Strait of Magellan, Southern Chile
slide2.body: 560km through Chilean Patagonia. Chile controls both shores. Argentina's southern territory comes close but never reaches a shore. This makes Magellan unique — genuine single-country control of a major international waterway.

slide3.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slide3.headline: The Only Calm Alternative To The Drake Passage.
slide3.body: For ships that can't survive the brutal Drake Passage, Magellan is the only alternative. LNG carriers from the Atlantic to the Pacific use it regularly. Chilean salmon and copper exports depend entirely on it.

slide4.label: THREAT LEVEL
slide4.headline: Argentina And Chile Nearly Went To War Here In 1978
slide4.body: The two countries came within hours of war over the nearby Beagle Channel. While a treaty was signed in 1984, the geopolitical tension of one country controlling the entire strait still lingers.

slide5.label: COLLATERAL DAMAGE
slide5.headline: Who Gets Hurt First
slide5.body: South America: Atlantic-Pacific trade disrupted. Global LNG: carriers forced to use the far more dangerous Drake route. Chilean exports: trapped at port. Argentina: loses its safest maritime connection to the Pacific.
